01Who Do They Answer To? · The whole system

The system runs as a circuit, from wealth back to wealth.

Read the five parts from left to right: wealth, voice, elections, checks and policy. Each passes influence to the next, and policy passes some of it back to wealth. Every connection carries a grade for how strong its evidence is.

01.4

Start from a question

Pick the question closest to your own life. Each one opens a short answer and the part of the system it runs through. There are five topics and 16 questions.

Cost of living

Why does it cost so much to live here?

  1. Why did my rent go up?Runs through Wealth, Your household and Technology · Loop R8

    Rent rises when more households compete for a limited number of homes where they need to live. City and town councils adopt zoning rules that set how many homes each lot may hold, and planning boards apply them project by project; in many high-demand regions those rules keep building below demand. Asking rents for professionally managed apartments were 29% higher in early 2026 than in 2020. For buyers, the monthly payment on a median-priced home rose from $1,240 at the end of 2020 to $2,420 in late 2025 as prices and mortgage rates climbed, and rates passed 7% in October 2026.

    Open loop R8, the housing-scarcity loop

  2. Why is my grocery bill higher?Runs through Wealth, Your household, Outside forces and Checks · Loops B3, R13

    Grocery prices are still rising slowly: the Consumer Price Index for food at home, the Bureau of Labor Statistics measure of grocery prices, rose 1.8% in the year to September 2026. Farms receive about 12 cents of each food dollar, so wages, fuel, transport and store costs set most of the price. Particular foods jump when supply shrinks, as eggs did during bird flu outbreaks and beef has as cattle numbers fell. Tariffs add a cost that U.S. importers mostly pay first. Whether large meatpackers and grocers use market power to widen margins is disputed; the Justice Department, the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general enforce the competition laws.

    Open loop B3, the new-competitor loop

  3. Why is my electric bill going up?Runs through Technology, Your household and Wealth

    Your rate is approved by a regulator or a board. For an investor-owned utility, the state public utility commission sets rates in a rate case; for public power and cooperatives, a city council, utility board or co-op board does. Rates recover the cost of power plants, fuel, transmission lines and local wires, and investor-owned utilities also earn a regulated return on what they invest. Recent increases trace mainly to grid spending, natural gas prices and disaster recovery. In the 13-state PJM grid region, a capacity auction overseen by federal regulators has added costs, and its market monitor attributes $23.1 billion over three auctions to data center demand.

    Open Technology

  4. Why did my home insurance premium go up?Runs through Your household, Outside forces and Wealth

    Home insurance costs more because each claim costs more to pay and more homes stand where storms and wildfires strike. Reinsurance, the coverage insurers buy for themselves, also became more expensive. Average monthly premiums rose 72% from 2019 to 2025, to $201. Insurers propose rates, and each state's insurance commissioner or department reviews them under rules the state legislature writes, including which costs may count. Where approved rates fall below expected losses, some insurers stop renewing policies and households turn to state-created insurers of last resort. Flood damage needs a separate policy, mostly from a federal program that Congress has extended through December 11, 2026.

    Open Your household

Health and care

Why is care so hard to get and to pay for?

  1. Why is it hard to find an appointment?Runs through Your household, Wealth, Checks and Technology · Loop B2

    An appointment depends on coverage and on whether a clinician near you has time. Whether you have coverage turns on your employer's plan, on marketplace subsidies that Congress sets, and on your state Medicaid agency, which checks eligibility at each renewal. Insurers then choose which clinicians join a plan's network. The number of clinicians nearby depends on Medicare funding for residency training, state licensing laws and what each payer pays. As of December 2025, 92.3 million people lived in federal primary care shortage areas. A 2025 survey of offices in 15 large metro areas, run by a staffing company, found an average wait of 31 days for a new patient.

    Open loop B2, the automatic-cushion loop

  2. Why can the same care produce different bills?Runs through Wealth, Your household and Checks · Loop B3

    Most of a medical bill's price comes from a private contract. Each insurer or employer plan negotiates its own rates with each hospital and clinician, so a scan can cost widely different amounts within one city. Hospitals with few nearby rivals win higher rates, and Medicare pays more for some services in hospital outpatient departments than in doctors' offices. RAND, a nonprofit research organization, found private plans paid hospitals 254% of Medicare rates in 2022. For medicines, the manufacturer sets a list price protected by patents, and pharmacy benefit managers negotiate rebates off that price, so a patient's coinsurance can still be based on the full list price.

    Open loop B3, the new-competitor loop

  3. Why does childcare cost so much, and why can't I find an opening?Runs through Your household and Wealth

    Childcare costs a lot because young children need many adults per child, and staff pay makes up most of a program's budget. State licensing agencies set those staff-to-child ratios. Pay stays low anyway: childcare workers earned a median $16.82 an hour in May 2025, and programs struggle to hire and keep staff. Parents cover most of the bill, an average of $13,184 a year in 2025 by the count of Child Care Aware of America, an advocacy group. Subsidies reached 16 percent of children eligible under federal rules in 2022, and each state legislature decides how much more to add.

    Open Your household

  4. Why is it so hard to get help at home as I age or live with a disability?Runs through Your household and Wealth

    Most paid long-term care runs through Medicaid, which paid 61 percent of the $415 billion spent in 2022 on long-term services, meaning help with daily tasks such as bathing and dressing. Federal Medicaid law requires states to cover nursing home care but leaves most home and community services optional, so states cap enrollment: more than 710,000 people were on waiting or interest lists in 2024. Medicare does not cover ongoing personal care. Home care depends on aides paid a median $17.21 an hour in May 2025, and family members fill the gaps. Each state's Medicaid agency decides who gets services and what providers are paid.

    Open Your household

Work and financial security

Why doesn't my paycheck go further?

  1. Why isn't my pay keeping up with what my work produces?Runs through Wealth and Your household · Loop R6

    Pay rises when workers produce more, though by less than the full gain, and bargaining power decides the split. In the U.S. nonfarm business sector, output per hour has grown about 2.1% a year since 1947. Workers' share of business income fell to 52.8% in the second quarter of 2026, the lowest on record. Your bargaining power depends on how easily you can leave for a better offer, how many employers compete to hire you, whether you can bargain as a group, and the legal wage floor. Congress, the National Labor Relations Board, state legislatures and state labor departments set or enforce most of those rules.

    Open loop R6, the bargaining-power loop

  2. How do taxes and benefit rules change what my household keeps?Runs through Your household and Wealth · Loops R5, B2

    What a household keeps depends on rules Congress writes and agencies carry out. Workers pay 7.65% of wages in payroll taxes for Social Security and Medicare from the first dollar. Federal income tax applies above the standard deduction, and refundable credits, which pay out even when no tax is owed, add money back for low earners with children. Benefits such as SNAP food aid and Medicaid shrink or end as earnings rise, so a raise can leave a family little better off. The Congressional Budget Office estimates that the 2025 federal law, Public Law 119-21, lowers resources for the lowest-income tenth of households and raises them for the top tenth.

    Open loop R5, the strained-household loop

  3. What will I get from Social Security, and could the rules change before I retire?Runs through Your household, Wealth and Checks

    Your benefit depends on your earnings record, the formula in the Social Security Act and the age you claim. The formula averages your highest 35 years of wage-indexed earnings and replaces a larger share of lower earnings. Benefits rise each year with inflation; the increase for 2027 is 3.6 percent. The 2026 Trustees Report projects that the retirement trust fund's reserves run out in late 2032, after which incoming taxes would cover 78 percent of scheduled benefits. Congress decides how to close that gap, and each option falls on different earners and birth years.

    Open Your household

Public services where you live

Who keeps the water, roads and schools working?

  1. Who makes sure my tap water is safe?Runs through Checks and Your household

    Your water utility tests and treats the water. It follows national limits set by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), and in most states a state drinking water program enforces them. The utility can be a city department, a regional authority or a private company. Customers' bills pay for most pipes and treatment: in 2017, state and local sources covered 96% of public spending on water utilities. A city council or utility board sets rates for most publicly owned systems, and a state utility commission regulates many private ones. For a problem, start with the utility. If it is not resolved, contact the state drinking water program.

    Open Checks

  2. Why is the repair on my street taking so long?Runs through Your household, Checks and Outside forces

    It depends first on who owns the road. Counties, cities and towns own about three-quarters of public road miles, and state transportation departments own most of the rest. A pothole waits for the local public works budget and crew schedule. Larger work that uses federal aid must be listed in a multi-year program adopted by the regional planning organization and approved by the governor, so it waits for money and its place in line. Federal money is under strain: CBO projects the highway account of the Highway Trust Fund will run out in 2028, and the 2021 infrastructure law covered fiscal years through 2026.

    Open Your household

  3. Why does my child's school have less than schools in other districts?Runs through Checks, Voice and Outside forces

    Most school money comes from local property taxes and state aid. In 2020-21, local sources supplied 44% of public school revenue and states 46%, and 83% of the local share came from property taxes. A district with more taxable property can raise more per student at the same tax rate. The state aid formula, written by the legislature, decides how much of that gap is closed, and state courts have ordered changes when formulas fall short of state constitutions. Studies comparing students before and after state finance reforms estimate that sustained increases raised schooling and adult earnings, most for children from low-income families.

    Open Checks

Voice, power and information

How do my vote and my voice reach the people who decide?

  1. Which election decides who represents me, and how can I influence the people who decide?Runs through Elections, Checks, Voice and Outside forces · Loops R10, B4, R4a, R4b, R12, R16, R11

    The election that decides an office is the one whose outcome is still in doubt. In a district one party wins reliably, that is the party primary, a nominating election often held months before November with far fewer voters. Cook Political Report rated 398 of 435 House seats safe for 2026. Unite America, an advocacy group, counts 383 as effectively decided in primaries, by 9.4% of eligible voters. State legislatures, or commissions in some states, draw the districts that make seats safe. Between elections, randomized experiments in two state legislatures found that constituent calls and emails about a specific bill changed legislators' votes.

    Open loop R10, the safe-seat loop

  2. How do algorithms affect the prices I pay, my job, what I see online and the services I get?Runs through Technology, Voice, Wealth and Checks · Loops R3, R7

    Companies and public agencies use software to set prices, screen job applicants, rank what you see online and decide benefit renewals, and the effects depend on the data fed in and the rules around it. Rent-pricing software that pooled competitors' private data led to a Justice Department case against RealPage. Large experiments found that changing a feed shifts what people see, with small measured effects on how they feel about the other party. Evidence on AI and jobs is early: one payroll study finds fewer jobs for workers aged 22 to 25 in exposed occupations, while others find no broad effect. Federal agencies, state legislatures and courts set the limits.

    Open loop R3, the outrage loop

00The conventions sheet

Every mark on these sheets makes one claim.

Every sheet in this atlas uses one small set of marks. A box is a condition that can rise or fall. An arrow says that one condition raises or lowers another. The rest of the marks say how sure the atlas is, how long the effect takes and where a reform would act.

00.1

The tip is the effect

An arrow runs from the condition that changes to the condition it moves. A plus sign means the two variables move the same way. It does not mean the change is good.

  • Raises, plus sign

    If the first condition rises, the second tends to rise too, other things held steady.

    Example: Safe seats make the primary decisive (L08).

  • Lowers, minus sign

    If the first condition rises, the second tends to fall. The minus sign does not mean harm.

    Example: Decisive primaries reduce general-election pressure (L25).

  • Decides, open diamond

    It says who decides, without saying which way the decision goes, so it has no sign and never closes a loop. The atlas has 7 of these.

    Example: Congress decides public investment levels (LE02).

00.2

Texture is the evidence

A solid line rests on the public record or strong research. Breaks in the line mean weaker evidence, down to dots for a claim nobody has tested. Line weight never shows size.

  • Documented

    On the public record. 32 connections.

  • Well supported

    Strong research evidence. 37 connections.

  • Plausible

    Some evidence. 35 connections.

  • Contested

    Evidence disputed. 7 connections.

  • Hypothesis

    Untested. 7 connections.

  • Hollow, a conceptual step

    A step in one of the three sketched loops. It is an idea with no numbered connection.

00.3

Ticks count the wait

Ticks sit just after the start of a line. The more ticks, the longer the change takes to arrive.

  • One tick

    Under 2 years. 38 connections.

  • Two ticks

    2 to 10 years. 45 connections.

  • Three ticks

    Over 10 years. 35 connections.

Multiply the signs around a loop. An even number of lowering steps makes it reinforcing: a change comes back stronger. An odd number makes it balancing: the loop pushes back. “Improvement or decline can reinforce itself.”

00.6

Red marks where a reform acts

A reform aims at named points: a connection, a condition, or both. On the loop and reform sheets, the one working red marks each point where reform R-01, the worked example, acts: the line and its arrowhead, or the box. An ink tag names each other reform that aims at the loop. Red does no other job on these sheets. Effects are rated family by family and never added up.

On the safe-seat loop, R-01 takes the red on its three targets: C2, L08, L25. This sample is a specimen.

00.7

How to read a card

Each part of the system appears on the overview as a card. Every card has the same sections in the same order, so the five read across like a table.

  1. Plain name, then the formal title
  2. The question this part answers
  3. What it is, in one sentence
  4. Every condition, with its code
  5. What it passes on along the circuit
  6. How many connections stay inside
  7. The loops based here

00.8

Words on these sheets

Variable
A quantity or condition in the model that can rise or fall. Its definition states what a higher or lower value means.
Connection
A claimed relationship between two variables. Its record explains the mechanism, gives the evidence grade and states the delay. Connection IDs begin with L, LE, LT, LX or T.
Feedback loop
A chain of causes that returns to its starting variable. Reinforcing loops amplify change and balancing loops counteract it; either kind can produce good or harmful results.
Reinforcing loop (R)
A feedback loop whose returning effect amplifies the first change. Improvement or decline can reinforce itself.
Balancing loop (B)
A feedback loop whose response pushes back against the first change. How well it works depends on whether each corrective step can act.
Outside driver
A force that affects the model but whose own causes lie outside its boundary, such as technology, population patterns, trade, foreign interference and major shocks.
Stock
An amount built up over time, such as wealth, debt, local news outlets or safe seats. It changes only through what flows in and out.
Flow
An amount arriving or leaving over a period, such as annual income or money spent per election cycle. Its time unit is part of the measure.
Delay
The time between a change and its effect. Codes: S, under 2 years; M, 2 to 10 years; L, over 10 years.
Documented
The confidence label for a fact or event on the public record: a statute, a court ruling or an official statistic. It establishes the event; it says nothing about the size of an effect unless the record does.
Well-supported
The confidence label for a relationship on which several credible studies, designed to rule out other explanations, agree about direction. Each study's setting and limits still apply.
Plausible
The confidence label for a coherent mechanism with some supporting evidence, where the studies are weak or few.
Contested
The confidence label for a relationship on which credible studies disagree. Both sides are shown with the connection.
Hypothesis
The confidence label for a proposed relationship that needs stronger evidence. Diagrams draw it as a dotted line, and it never serves as the only support for a claim.
Reform profile
One of 50 entries, R-01 to R-50, describing a proposed change: the connections it aims at, the routes it can travel, what it depends on, separate evidence about the problem and the remedy, expected directions for each outcome family, and how it could fail.
Problem evidence
Evidence that the condition or mechanism a reform addresses exists. It is graded separately from remedy evidence.
Remedy evidence
Evidence that an intervention changes the condition it targets, with attention to where and how it was carried out.
Feasibility
A judgment of whether a route to change is open under present political and legal conditions. The Atlas rates it high, medium, low or very low for 2026 to 2030.

02Part C · A close-up

Elections

Electoral competition. Who picks them?

Accountability depends on a real chance of losing. In most districts the general election is easy to predict, so the contest that decides the seat is a low-turnout primary. Incumbents also help write the rules for their own races, from district maps to voting procedures. When few officials face a competitive race, the pressure to serve the whole electorate fades.

  • Contested evidence disputed
  • Hypothesis untested

02.1

The five conditions

Each condition can rise or fall. The bold line says what a higher value means, so a label such as “Safe seats” reads as an amount.

VariableC1

Seats with little electoral competition

Districts where one party wins by a wide margin, so its candidates face little risk in the general election. The model counts seats won by more than 10 percentage points.

A higher value means more seats are safe for one party.

Loops
R10, R12, R4a
Issues
21
VariableC2

How often the primary decides the winner

The share of seats where the general election is so predictable that the primary settles who takes office. Turnout in that deciding contest can be far lower than in November.

A higher value means more seats are settled in the primary.

Loops
R10
Issues
11
VariableC3

Risk of losing office

The credible threat that an incumbent will lose the next election. Where seats are competitive, the threat pushes officials to respond to voters before anyone is removed.

A higher value means incumbents face a more credible chance of defeat.

Loops
B4, R10, R11, R16
Issues
26
VariableC4

Officeholders' control over election rules

The power of people already in office to set district maps, voting-access rules and local election choices. This is rule-setting authority, and each rule's effect needs its own evidence.

A higher value means incumbents have more say over the rules of their own elections.

Loops
R10, R12, R4a, R4b
Issues
27
VariableC5

Incumbents defeated or pushed into retirement

Officeholders who lose an election or retire under threat of defeat. This consequence is measured separately from the pressure they face while still in office.

A higher value means more incumbents lose or retire under threat of defeat in an election cycle.

Loops
B4
Issues
11

02.3

Loops that run through it

Seven loops run through Elections. Risk of losing office (C3) and Incumbents control election rules (C4) each sit on four of them, more than any other condition here.

Two loops meet at risk of losing office (C3): the accountability loop (B4), which pushes back, and the safe-seat loop (R10), which feeds itself. The accountability loop works only where seats are competitive. R10 starts from safe seats (C1).

A legislative majority draws district maps that make many of its seats safe.

02.4

Issues tracked here

39 active issue records touch C1 to C5. Each names a problem in plain words, grades its evidence and gives a real place where it happened. Open any row for the full record.

Showing 39

IDIssueOnEvidenceReal-world example
  1. I001Local newsrooms close and fewer reporters watch local governmentC3 Well supportedGallup, New Mexico, loses its paper after 62 years

    When a local paper or station closes, fewer reporters attend council meetings, read budgets or question officials. Residents lose a shared source of facts about local decisions, and local officials face less public scrutiny.

    Where it happened

    Gallup, New Mexico, loses its paper after 62 years Gallup, New Mexico, 2026.

    In January 2026, the Gallup Independent in Gallup, New Mexico, printed its last issue after 62 years. Its circulation had fallen from 18,000 in 2006 to under 5,000. Bob Zollinger, whose family ran the paper, worries the city council and county commission will now meet with no reporter present. Source: Source NM, 2026.

    A fix tried elsewhere

    New Jersey funds local news through a state-created consortium New Jersey, 2018-2026.

    New Jersey's 2018 law created the Civic Information Consortium, a nonprofit that funds local journalism with donations and state money. It has issued more than $12 million in grants. State support fell from $4 million in fiscal 2024 to $2.5 million in fiscal 2026, and Gov. Mikie Sherrill's first budget proposal would zero it out. Source: New Jersey Monitor, 2026.

    Evidence
    Well supported. The 2025 State of Local News census counted 212 U.S. counties with no local news source (the report's landing page gives 213). A 2020 study by Gao, Lee and Murphy linked newspaper closures to higher borrowing costs for local governments. Hayes and Lawless (2021) found that shrinking local coverage goes with lower political engagement and knowledge; their panel and content data support associations, and the authors limit their causal claims.
    Proposed response
    State legislatures and local philanthropies would create an independently governed local-news fund. It would pay formula grants, keep funders away from editorial decisions and publish data on every award. (State legislatures; local philanthropies)
    Tradeoff
    Public money can invite political control of coverage. The design keeps the people who appoint the fund's board separate from the people who make editorial decisions.
    How to tell it works
    Counties with a local news source, reporters per resident, and the corrections that funded outlets publish.
    Reforms aimed at it
    • R-32 Pays reporters to cover local government with an editorial firewall, which is the fund this record proposes.
  2. I002Chain owners cut local reportingC3 PlausibleStations bought by Sinclair shift toward national politics

    When one company buys many local papers or stations, it often cuts local staff and shares content across its outlets. The strongest study, of one TV station owner, found coverage moved toward national politics and viewers left.

    Where it happened

    Stations bought by Sinclair shift toward national politics Seven U.S. TV markets served by former Bonten stations, 2017.

    In September 2017, Sinclair Broadcast Group finished buying 14 local TV stations from Bonten Media Group. A study in the American Political Science Review found the stations' coverage of national politics rose about 25% while local politics coverage fell. Their coverage also moved to the right, and a small drop in viewership was not statistically significant. Source: American Political Science Review (Martin and McCrain), 2019.

    A fix tried elsewhere

    Regulators' review stops Sinclair's bid for Tribune Media United States, 2018.

    In July 2018, the Federal Communications Commission sent Sinclair's $3.9 billion bid for Tribune Media to a hearing before a judge. Commissioners questioned whether planned sales of stations to buyers close to Sinclair were a sham that would let Sinclair keep running them. Tribune walked away from the deal in August. Source: CNN Business, 2018.

    Evidence
    Plausible. Martin and McCrain (2019, American Political Science Review) found that local TV stations bought by Sinclair shifted toward national and right-leaning political coverage and lost viewers. The study covers one ownership group. Staff cuts at chain-owned outlets appear in industry counts such as the 2025 State of Local News report.
    Proposed response
    Congress, the Federal Communications Commission and the federal antitrust agencies would review local news mergers for their effect on competition and on the number of independent outlets. Owners would disclose who ultimately owns each outlet and how many newsroom staff it employs. (Congress; FCC; antitrust agencies)
    Tradeoff
    Owning many outlets proves neither biased coverage nor illegal market power, so each deal needs its own evidence.
    How to tell it works
    More distinct owners in each local market and more original local reporting.
    Reforms aimed at it
    • R-32 Funds independent local reporters, which offsets the staff cuts that follow acquisitions; ownership itself stays unchanged.
  3. I003Platforms take the advertising that once paid for reportingC3 Well supportedJudge finds Google illegally dominated online ad tools

    Most of the advertising money that used to support newspapers now goes to large online platforms. News organizations still pay the cost of reporting, so they cover fewer public decisions.

    Where it happened

    Judge finds Google illegally dominated online ad tools United States (federal court in Alexandria, Virginia), 2025-2026.

    In April 2025, a federal judge in Virginia ruled that Google held an illegal monopoly over some of the technology websites use to sell ads. Publishers pay a 20% fee on Google's ad exchange. In September 2026 the judge ordered six years of rule changes and declined to force a sale, and Google said it would appeal. Source: Reuters (republished by The Star), 2026.

    A fix tried elsewhere

    Canada tried a tax credit for news subscriptions Canada, 2020.

    Canada let taxpayers claim a credit worth 15% of up to $500 spent on qualifying digital news subscriptions. About 302,000 people filed for it in 2020, roughly 1% of the country's more than 27 million tax filers, and the average credit was $36. Source: Nieman Lab, 2022.

    Evidence
    Well supported. Industry estimates compiled by the Pew Research Center show U.S. newspaper advertising revenue falling from about $49 billion in 2005 to under $10 billion in 2022. The 2025 State of Local News census counted 212 counties with no local news source.
    Proposed response
    A state legislature would pilot reader vouchers and refundable tax credits for local news subscriptions. Nonprofit and small independent outlets would qualify alongside established publishers. (State legislature)
    Tradeoff
    Subsidies can flow mostly to large, established publishers. Eligibility rules need to be neutral about viewpoint and simple enough for small outlets to use.
    How to tell it works
    New subscribers, readers reached in places with little coverage, and public cost per reader.
    Reforms aimed at it
    • R-32 Replaces part of the lost advertising money with public and philanthropic funding behind an editorial firewall.
    • R-44 Opens search and ad-tech markets so a smaller share of advertising money is captured by a few platforms.
  4. I013Public records arrive too late to be usefulC3 DocumentedFederal records backlog jumps by a third in 2024

    Federal agencies take weeks or months to answer requests for public records, and backlogs keep growing. Slow answers stall investigations by reporters and residents.

    Where it happened

    Federal records backlog jumps by a third in 2024 United States (federal agencies), 2024.

    In fiscal 2024, the backlog of overdue federal Freedom of Information Act requests grew 33%, to 267,056, by the Brechner Center's count of federal data. Simple requests took 44 days on average, up from 39 the year before. Agencies spent an estimated $723 million processing requests. Source: Brechner Center for Freedom of Information, University of Florida, 2025.

    Evidence
    Documented. The Justice Department reported 1.50 million federal Freedom of Information Act requests in fiscal year 2024, up 25%, with simple requests taking 44 days on average, the longest since 2011. A tabulation of FOIA.gov data by the Brechner Center counted a year-end backlog of 267,056 requests, up 33%, and a record-low 12% of requests granted in full.
    Proposed response
    Congress, federal agencies and the states would fund records officers, publish records openly in machine-readable form and enforce response deadlines with an appeal that works. (Congress; agencies; states)
    Tradeoff
    Redactions still have to protect privacy and legitimate security interests.
    How to tell it works
    Age of the request backlog, and how complete agencies' proactive publication is.
  5. I017Registration hurdles and roll errors keep eligible people from votingC4 Well supportedBrooklyn voters wrongly dropped before a 2016 primary

    Eligible people can miss an election because registering is hard or because their record was wrongly removed from the rolls. The burden falls hardest on people who move often.

    Where it happened

    Brooklyn voters wrongly dropped before a 2016 primary Brooklyn, New York City, New York, 2016.

    New York City's Board of Elections removed more than 117,000 Brooklyn voters from the rolls before the 2016 presidential primary. In a 2017 consent decree the board admitted it broke state and federal law. It agreed to review removals back to 2013 and restore voters it had wrongly purged. Source: WNYC, 2017.

    A fix tried elsewhere

    Oregon registers voters automatically at the DMV Oregon, 2016.

    Oregon began registering people automatically when they visited the Department of Motor Vehicles, under a 2015 law. More than 230,000 people were added through the program by the 2016 election, and 97,184 of them voted for president. Source: Stateline (Pew Charitable Trusts), 2016.

    Evidence
    Well supported. The Brennan Center for Justice, a voting-rights research and advocacy organization, counted about 16 million voters removed from rolls nationwide between 2014 and 2016, with removal rates rising in places formerly covered by federal preclearance after Shelby County v. Holder (2013). These are removal rates. The count does not show how many removals were mistakes.
    Proposed response
    States, and Congress for federal elections, would adopt automatic and same-day registration, keep rolls accurate with secure methods, and give voters notice and a chance to correct their record before any removal. (Congress for federal elections; states)
    Tradeoff
    Rules must protect eligibility checks and data security, and keep noncitizens from being enrolled by mistake.
    How to tell it works
    Share of eligible people registered, wrongful removals, and provisional ballots accepted.
    Reforms aimed at it
    • R-05 Registers eligible people through routine dealings with state agencies, removing the registration step that falls hardest on people who move.
  6. I018Long lines make voting cost more in some neighborhoodsC4 Well supportedMaricopa County cut polling places and lines stretched hours

    In some places voters wait far longer to cast a ballot, often because their polling places get fewer machines and staff. Waiting costs the most for people who cannot leave work.

    Where it happened

    Maricopa County cut polling places and lines stretched hours Maricopa County, Arizona, 2016.

    Maricopa County, Arizona, opened 60 polling places for its March 2016 presidential primary, down from about 200 four years earlier. One Phoenix voter waited more than five hours, and some people were still in line at midnight. County Recorder Helen Purcell told supervisors she took full responsibility for the cut. Source: Cronkite News (Arizona PBS), 2016.

    A fix tried elsewhere

    Georgia ties precinct size to hour-long lines Georgia, 2021 to 2026.

    Georgia's 2021 voting law requires action when voters wait more than an hour at an Election Day precinct. Officials must then cut the number of voters assigned there to no more than 2,000. Election Day lines have been rare in Georgia since the chaotic 2020 primary, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported in 2026. Source: Atlanta Journal-Constitution, 2026.

    Evidence
    Well supported. Using smartphone location data from the 2016 election, Chen, Haggag, Pope and Rohla (2019) found that residents of Black neighborhoods waited 29% longer to vote than residents of white neighborhoods; the measurement is strong and covers one election. Pettigrew (2017), working from surveys and observational data, found that minority voters wait longer and traced the gap to how local officials allocate precinct resources. A 2014 Government Accountability Office review of the 2012 election reported that some voters waited over an hour.
    Proposed response
    States and local election offices would set service standards for polling-place access, early voting and mail voting, fund the staff needed to meet them and track the results. (States; local election offices)
    Tradeoff
    Costs and geography differ from place to place, and any expansion has to keep a secure chain of custody for ballots.
    How to tell it works
    Wait times by precinct, and ballot rejection rates.
  7. I019Voters with disabilities and limited English face barriers to voting on their ownC4 DocumentedHarris County polling places had barriers for disabled voters

    Some voters with disabilities cannot cast a private ballot without help, and some voters who need language assistance do not receive it. Each voting method needs testing with the people who use it.

    Where it happened

    Harris County polling places had barriers for disabled voters Harris County, Texas, 2019.

    Harris County, Texas, had more than 750 polling places in 2019, the third-largest voting program in the country. The Justice Department alleged that many had barriers such as steep ramps and locked gates. A 2019 settlement required the county to survey nearly two-thirds of its sites and offer effective curbside voting. Source: U.S. Department of Justice, 2019.

    A fix tried elsewhere

    Ballots in voters' own languages raised participation U.S. counties and towns covered by the Voting Rights Act's language provisions, 2012 election (study published 2016).

    The Voting Rights Act requires counties and towns with sizable language-minority populations to provide ballots and help in those languages. Studying 1,465 jurisdictions in the 2012 election, political scientists Bernard Fraga and Julie Lee Merseth compared places just above and just below the coverage cutoff. Source: Fraga and Merseth, Journal of Race, Ethnicity, and Politics (Cambridge University Press), 2016.

    Evidence
    Documented. The U.S. Election Assistance Commission's survey series found that the turnout gap between voters with and without disabilities fell from 16.8 points in 2000 to 11.3 points in 2020, with difficulties persisting. In a sample of 178 polling places in 2016, the Government Accountability Office found that 60% had at least one impediment to access.
    Proposed response
    Election administrators would audit every voting method for disability access and provide the language assistance the law requires, testing each with the voters who use it. The Justice Department would enforce these duties. (Election administrators; DOJ)
    Tradeoff
    Accessible voting technology needs security protections and a backup method.
    How to tell it works
    Voters with disabilities who vote independently and successfully, and accessibility complaints.
  8. I020Conviction rules keep millions from votingC4 DocumentedFlorida tied restored voting rights to paying court debts

    About 4 million Americans could not vote in 2024 because of a felony conviction, under rules that differ by state. Lifetime bans, confusing eligibility and payment conditions keep many excluded after release.

    Where it happened

    Florida tied restored voting rights to paying court debts Florida, 2018 to 2020.

    Florida voters restored voting rights to most people with felony convictions in 2018. The next year lawmakers required them to settle all fines and restitution first. In 2020 a federal appeals court upheld that rule 6-4, leaving people who cannot pay their court debts unable to vote. Source: Associated Press (via Boston Globe), 2020.

    A fix tried elsewhere

    Minnesota restored the vote on release from prison Minnesota, 2023 to 2024.

    Minnesota's 2023 law restores voting rights to people with felony convictions once they leave prison, instead of after probation ends. An estimated 55,000 people gained the right to vote. In August 2024 the Minnesota Supreme Court rejected a challenge to the law. Source: Associated Press, 2024.

    Evidence
    Documented. The Sentencing Project, an advocacy organization, estimated that about 4.0 million people were barred from voting by a felony conviction in 2024, including 4.5% of Black adults compared with 1.3% of other adults. The estimate comes from a model built on correctional data.
    Proposed response
    States, and Congress where it has authority, would restore voting rights on release from prison, notify eligible people automatically and remove payment conditions that make voting depend on wealth. (States; Congress where authorized)
    Tradeoff
    Eligibility law varies by state, and constitutional litigation may be needed.
    How to tell it works
    Registrations by people whose rights were restored, and eligibility errors.
  9. I021DC and territorial residents have no vote in CongressC1 C2 C3 C4 C5 DocumentedCongress overturned a DC law without a DC vote

    About 700,000 people in Washington, DC, along with residents of the U.S. territories, have no voting member of the House or Senate. Changing that takes legislation or a constitutional amendment, and territorial residents' own choices about political status.

    Where it happened

    Congress overturned a DC law without a DC vote Washington, DC, 2023.

    In March 2023, the House voted 250-173 to overturn the District of Columbia's rewrite of its criminal code, and the Senate and President Biden followed. Congress had not nullified a DC law this way in more than three decades. DC's only member of Congress, Delegate Eleanor Holmes Norton, holds a nonvoting seat. Source: Associated Press, 2023.

    A fix tried elsewhere

    A 1961 amendment gave DC a vote for president Washington, DC, 1961.

    The Twenty-third Amendment, ratified on March 29, 1961, gave District of Columbia residents presidential electors, capped at the number held by the least populous state. DC residents first voted for president in 1964. The amendment left them without a voting member of Congress. Source: National Archives (Reagan Library blog), 2022.

    Evidence
    Documented. The Census Bureau puts the District of Columbia's population at about 700,000, and the District has no voting member of the House or Senate.
    Proposed response
    Congress would pursue representation for DC and a political status for each territory chosen by its residents, through lawful legislation and, where needed, a constitutional amendment. (Congress; affected residents)
    Tradeoff
    Residents' consent, the constitutional structure and territorial self-determination all have to be respected.
    How to tell it works
    Residents with full voting representation in Congress.
  10. I022Map-drawers lock in a party's seatsC1 C3 C4 C5 Well supportedBoth parties drew congressional maps to win seats

    Officials who draw district lines can arrange them so their party keeps its seats even as voters change their minds. Federal courts do not hear these claims, so state rules and commissions decide how far it goes.

    Where it happened

    Both parties drew congressional maps to win seats North Carolina and Maryland, 2011 to 2019.

    In North Carolina, Republican legislator David Lewis proposed a 2016 congressional map electing 10 Republicans and 3 Democrats, and Republicans won 10 of 13 seats. Maryland Democrats in 2011 moved about 360,000 voters out of one district to flip it. In Rucho v. Common Cause (2019), the Supreme Court ruled federal courts cannot hear such claims. Source: Supreme Court of the United States, 2019.

    A fix tried elsewhere

    Arizona voters handed map-drawing to an independent commission Arizona, 2000 to 2015.

    Arizona voters adopted Proposition 106 in 2000, moving congressional map-drawing from the legislature to an independent commission. No more than two of its five members may belong to the same party, and the chair must come from outside those parties. The legislature sued, and in 2015 the Supreme Court upheld the commission 5-4. Source: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School (Supreme Court opinion), 2015.

    Evidence
    Well supported. In Rucho v. Common Cause (2019), the Supreme Court ruled that federal courts cannot hear partisan gerrymandering claims; state law and other federal voting protections still apply. Warshaw, McGhee and Migurski (2022) found that maps drawn by commissions and courts in the 2021 to 2022 cycle showed less partisan bias than maps drawn by legislatures, using descriptive measures from one cycle. The Congressional Research Service has documented the mid-decade redraws of 2025 and 2026.
    Proposed response
    States, and Congress for House elections, would give map-drawing to independent commissions, publish draft maps, set explicit neutral criteria and allow enforceable review in state courts. (States; Congress for House rules)
    Tradeoff
    Geography limits how many districts can be competitive, and neutral criteria can conflict with protecting minority voters' ability to elect candidates.
    How to tell it works
    Partisan bias measured across a range of possible vote outcomes, and districts where minority voters can elect their preferred candidates.
    Reforms aimed at it
    • R-04 Moves map-drawing away from the majority whose seats the map would protect.
    • R-03 Proportional counting in multi-member districts makes seat shares follow vote shares, so district lines matter less.
  11. I023District lines and at-large elections can dilute minority votesC1 C4 DocumentedAlabama's map gave Black voters one district of seven

    How districts are drawn, or electing a whole council at large, can keep a protected racial group from electing its preferred candidates. After the Supreme Court's 2026 Callais decision, the legal standard for a remedy is much harder to meet.

    Where it happened

    Alabama's map gave Black voters one district of seven Alabama, 2021 to 2023.

    Alabama's 2021 congressional map had seven districts and only one in which Black voters made up a majority of the voting-age population. A three-judge federal court found the map likely violated the Voting Rights Act. In Allen v. Milligan (2023), the Supreme Court affirmed that finding. Source: Supreme Court of the United States, 2023.

    A fix tried elsewhere

    Louisiana's second Black-majority district was struck down Louisiana, 2024 to 2026.

    After a federal judge found in 2022 that Louisiana's congressional map likely violated the Voting Rights Act, the state enacted a new map, SB8, with a second majority-Black district. In Louisiana v. Callais, decided April 29, 2026, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that SB8 was an unconstitutional racial gerrymander. Source: Supreme Court of the United States, 2026.

    Evidence
    Documented. In Allen v. Milligan (2023), the Supreme Court found that Alabama's congressional map likely diluted Black votes under Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act. Shelby County v. Holder (2013) struck down the formula that decided which places needed federal approval before changing voting rules, leaving the rest of the Act in place. Louisiana v. Callais (April 29, 2026) revised how courts analyze Section 2 districting claims; it left Section 2 in force and did not bar every majority-minority district.
    Proposed response
    Congress, the Justice Department, the states and the courts would enforce voting-rights protections and adopt district or proportional remedies that have held up in court, with input from affected communities. (Congress; DOJ; states; courts)
    Tradeoff
    Each case and remedy has to be checked against current doctrine. Callais changes Section 2 districting standards substantially, so a current analysis of race and party voting patterns has to come before any remedy is designed.
    How to tell it works
    Whether protected groups can elect their preferred candidates, and gaps in access to voting.
    Reforms aimed at it
    • R-03 Proportional counting lets a cohesive group win seats in proportion to its votes without depending on single-district lines.
  12. I024Winner-take-all districts can leave large groups of voters with few seatsC1 C2 C3 C4 C5 DocumentedSingle-seat districts turned close votes into lopsided delegations

    When the top vote-getter takes a district's only seat, a party with substantial support across a state can win few of that state's seats. Nationally the 2024 House result was close to each party's vote share; the gaps appear inside individual states and in uncontested seats.

    Where it happened

    Single-seat districts turned close votes into lopsided delegations North Carolina and Maryland, 2012 to 2018.

    In 2016, Republican House candidates in North Carolina won 10 of 13 seats with 53% of the statewide vote. In Maryland, Democrats won 7 of 8 seats in every election from 2012 to 2018 while never topping 65% of the vote. Justice Elena Kagan cited both results in her dissent in Rucho v. Common Cause. Source: Supreme Court of the United States, 2019.

    Evidence
    Documented. Federal law (2 U.S.C. 2c) requires single-member House districts, so each state's delegation is chosen one winner-take-all seat at a time. Nationally the 2024 split of House seats came close to the split of votes; the disproportion shows up in individual states and in seats without major-party competition.
    Proposed response
    Congress would authorize multi-member House districts elected by single transferable vote or another tested proportional method. State legislatures would draw them and keep protections for minority voters. (Congress; state legislatures)
    Tradeoff
    Party competition and the way members serve constituents would change, and voters and officials would need education and tested ballots. The post-Callais legal framework has to be checked before adoption.
    How to tell it works
    How closely each state's seat shares match its vote shares, and whether voters have meaningful choices.
    Reforms aimed at it
    • R-03 Multi-member districts with proportional counting are the direct response to winner-take-all seat distortion.
  13. I025Similar candidates split the vote and push voters off their first choiceC1 C2 C3 C4 C5 Well supportedMaine elected a governor with 38% of the vote

    When two similar candidates run, they can divide their supporters and let a third candidate win with less than a majority. Voters who see this coming often abandon their favorite to avoid helping the candidate they like least.

    Where it happened

    Maine elected a governor with 38% of the vote Maine, 2010.

    In Maine's 2010 race for governor, Republican Paul LePage won with 38% of the vote in a divided field of four candidates. The National Conference of State Legislatures notes the race is often cited when supporters of ranked-choice voting argue that candidates should need at least 50% of the vote to win. Source: National Conference of State Legislatures, 2026.

    A fix tried elsewhere

    Maine now ranks candidates in primaries and federal races Maine, 2018 to present.

    Maine first used ranked-choice voting in its June 12, 2018 primary. Voters now rank candidates in all state primaries and in general elections for federal offices, including president. A 2017 advisory opinion from Maine's highest court said the state constitution bars it in general elections for governor and the legislature. Source: Maine Secretary of State, Bureau of Corporations, Elections and Commissions, 2026.

    Evidence
    Well supported. The spoiler effect follows from the counting rule: when only first choices count, supporters of two similar candidates divide their votes. The sources listed for this record study the ranked alternative and give no count of U.S. races decided by a spoiler.
    Proposed response
    States and cities would pilot single-winner ranked-choice voting or another majority method, with clear counting rules, full release of ballot data and audits. (States; cities)
    Tradeoff
    Ranked counting leaves some ballots exhausted and can produce nonmonotonic results, where ranking a candidate higher causes that candidate to lose. It elects one winner per seat, so it leaves proportional representation unchanged.
    How to tell it works
    Ballot errors, exhausted ballots, and a published definition of the support a winner needs.
    Reforms aimed at it
    • R-02 Ranked ballots transfer to a later choice, which removes the penalty for running or voting for a similar candidate. Disclosure. Oath & Action's editor works with the Yes on 3 campaign for Massachusetts Question 3 and promotes it through Veterans for All Voters, where he is Massachusetts state lead. He also co-leads Ranked Choice Melrose, a local campaign.
    • R-47 Fusion voting lets two parties nominate the same candidate, so allied parties can combine support instead of splitting it. Disclosure. Oath & Action's editor works with the Yes on 3 campaign for Massachusetts Question 3 and promotes it through Veterans for All Voters, where he is Massachusetts state lead. He also co-leads Ranked Choice Melrose, a local campaign.
  14. I026Closed primaries shut unaffiliated voters out of the deciding electionC1 C2 C3 C4 C5 DocumentedMillions of independents locked out of 2024 primaries

    In a closed primary only voters enrolled in a party can help choose its nominee. Where the primary effectively decides the seat, unaffiliated voters have no say in the contest that settles it.

    Where it happened

    Millions of independents locked out of 2024 primaries 15 states with closed primaries, 2024.

    Unite America, a group that campaigns for open primaries, counted 15.7 million registered independents in 15 states who could not vote in their state's closed primaries in 2024. The group estimated that 87% of U.S. House races were effectively decided in primaries that year. Source: Unite America, 2024.

    A fix tried elsewhere

    Alaska opened its primary to every voter Alaska, 2020 to 2026.

    Alaska voters approved an initiative in the 2020 general election creating a nonpartisan primary in which each voter picks one candidate per race, regardless of party. The four candidates with the most votes advance to a ranked-choice general election. The primary was first used on August 16, 2022. Source: Alaska Division of Elections, 2026.

    Evidence
    Documented. Ballotpedia's 2026 state-by-state count classifies each state's primary as closed, semi-closed, open, top-two or top-four. California and Washington use top-two primaries, and Alaska uses a top-four primary with a ranked general election. As of October 15, 2026, Massachusetts Question 3, on the November 3, 2026 ballot, would replace party primaries with a single primary in which the top two finishers advance, without ranked ballots.
    Proposed response
    States and parties would compare semi-open primaries, nonpartisan qualifying elections and party-run nominations, judged by who participates and what choices voters get. (States; parties)
    Tradeoff
    Parties have a constitutional right of association that limits how far states can open their nominations, and evidence that open primaries produce more moderate legislators is mixed.
    How to tell it works
    Participation among eligible voters, the range of candidates, and how well voters understand the ballot.
    Reforms aimed at it
    • R-01 An all-party primary lets every voter take part in the contest that narrows the field. Disclosure. Oath & Action's editor works with the Yes on 3 campaign for Massachusetts Question 3 and promotes it through Veterans for All Voters, where he is Massachusetts state lead. He also co-leads Ranked Choice Melrose, a local campaign.
  15. I027Ballot-access rules make it harder for new candidates to runC1 C2 C3 C4 PlausibleOhio made independents file 229 days before the election

    States set signature counts, fees and filing deadlines for getting on the ballot, and these are often heavier for minor parties and independents. High hurdles can keep credible challengers out of a race.

    Where it happened

    Ohio made independents file 229 days before the election Ohio, 1980.

    Ohio required independent presidential candidates in 1980 to file by March 20, 229 days before the election and months before the major parties picked nominees. John Anderson declared his independent run on April 24, 1980, after the deadline had passed. He and his supporters sued over the rule. Source: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School (Supreme Court opinion), 1983.

    A fix tried elsewhere

    The Supreme Court struck down Ohio's early deadline Ohio, 1983.

    In Anderson v. Celebrezze (1983), the Supreme Court ruled, with four Justices dissenting, that Ohio's March deadline placed an unconstitutional burden on the voting and associational rights of Anderson's supporters. The Court said such a burden discriminates against voters whose political preferences lie outside the existing parties. Source: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School (Supreme Court opinion), 1983.

    Evidence
    Plausible. Ballotpedia's 2026 state-by-state tables document signature and fee requirements that are heavier for minor-party and independent candidates than for major-party nominees. The tables show the rules; no study listed for this record measures how many credible candidates they deter.
    Proposed response
    States would set signature thresholds in proportion to the size of the electorate and uniform filing deadlines. Debate sponsors would adopt neutral criteria for who gets on stage. (States; debate sponsors)
    Tradeoff
    Thresholds set too low lengthen ballots and add work for election offices.
    How to tell it works
    Candidates who qualify, signatures rejected, and how many viewers debates reach.
  16. I028Equal Senate seats give small-state residents more weightC1 C4 DocumentedNo example in V7

    Every state has two senators whatever its population, so a resident of a small state has far more Senate representation per person than a resident of a large one. Article V of the Constitution bars changing a state's equal Senate vote without that state's consent.

    Evidence
    Documented. The 2020 Census counted California at about 39.5 million residents and Wyoming at about 577,000, roughly 68 to 1, and each state elects two senators.
    Proposed response
    Congress and the states would analyze options for admitting states and for representation, and would pursue any constitutional change toward population equality with Article V's limits stated openly. (Congress; states)
    Tradeoff
    Article V protects each state's equal Senate vote unless that state consents to a change.
    How to tell it works
    Residents per senator across states, and the size of the representation gap.
    Reforms aimed at it
    • R-50 Keeps Senate apportionment options under examination with Article V's constraints explicit.
  17. I029The Electoral College can elect the national vote's runner-upC1 C2 C3 C4 C5 DocumentedBush won in 2000 with fewer popular votes than Gore

    Because most states give all their electoral votes to the statewide winner, a candidate can win the presidency with fewer votes nationwide. The alternatives, a constitutional amendment or an interstate compact, each carry legal questions.

    Where it happened

    Bush won in 2000 with fewer popular votes than Gore United States (decided by Florida), 2000.

    In 2000, George W. Bush won the presidency with 271 electoral votes to Al Gore's 266, though Gore received more popular votes nationwide, the National Archives notes. Bush carried all 25 of Florida's electoral votes, which put him past the 270 needed. Source: National Archives, 2000.

    A fix tried elsewhere

    Eighteen states and DC signed a popular-vote compact 18 states and the District of Columbia, 2026.

    Eighteen states and the District of Columbia have enacted the National Popular Vote compact, which would award their electoral votes to the national vote winner. By the count of National Popular Vote, the group promoting it, members hold 222 electoral votes. It takes effect only once members reach 270. Source: National Popular Vote, 2026.

    Evidence
    Documented. In the 2000 and 2016 presidential elections, the Electoral College winner received fewer popular votes nationwide than the runner-up.
    Proposed response
    Congress and the states would compare direct popular election by constitutional amendment with the interstate compact, planning for litigation and for how each would operate. (Congress; states)
    Tradeoff
    The compact's validity and operation remain contested, and no simple federal statute can replace the Electoral College nationwide.
    How to tell it works
    Whether the presidential winner matches the national popular-vote winner, and how widely campaigns spread their attention across states.
    Reforms aimed at it
    • R-50 Covers both an Electoral College amendment and the National Popular Vote compact.
  18. I030Threats and pressure drive election officials outC3 C4 C5 Well supportedNearly 4 in 10 local election officials report threats

    Local election officials face threats and pressure over counting and certifying results, duties the law defines. Experienced staff leave, and the personal cost of serving rises.

    Where it happened

    Nearly 4 in 10 local election officials report threats United States (local election offices), 2025.

    In a Brennan Center survey of 858 local election officials taken in April and May 2025, 38% said they had faced threats, harassment or abuse because of their job. More than half, 52%, said they were concerned about the safety of their colleagues and staff. Source: Brennan Center for Justice, 2025.

    Evidence
    Well supported. In the Brennan Center's survey of 858 local election officials (April to May 2025), 38% reported threats, harassment or abuse, 52% worried about their staff's safety and 60% worried about federal cuts to election security support.
    Proposed response
    States, Congress and the Justice Department would professionalize election administration, protect certification as a defined legal duty and fund threat response under public standards. (States; Congress; DOJ)
    Tradeoff
    Independent election offices still need accountable appointments and public audits.
    How to tell it works
    Vacancies in election offices, threats reported, and certifications completed on time and as the law requires.
    Reforms aimed at it
    • R-45 Protects election officials and makes certification a scheduled legal duty.
  19. I031Election offices run on irregular fundingC3 C5 PlausibleFederal election security grants rise and fall each year

    U.S. elections cost about $2 billion a year, paid mostly by local governments on an irregular basis. Old equipment and staff turnover raise the risk of errors and security problems.

    Where it happened

    Federal election security grants rise and fall each year United States, 2018 to 2026.

    Congress has funded federal election security grants to states only in some years since 2018, with no new money in 2019 or 2021. It appropriated $15 million for fiscal 2025 and $45 million for fiscal 2026, and states must add a 20% match. Source: U.S. Election Assistance Commission, 2026.

    Evidence
    Plausible. The MIT Election Data and Science Lab's 2021 synthesis estimated that elections cost roughly $2 billion a year nationally, with funding that is local and irregular. In the Brennan Center's 2025 survey of 858 local election officials, 60% worried about federal cuts to security support. Neither source measures error rates.
    Proposed response
    Congress and the states would provide recurring formula grants for paper records, risk-limiting audits, cybersecurity and trained staff. (Congress; states)
    Tradeoff
    Federal requirements should come with funding, and equipment contracts should avoid locking offices into one vendor.
    How to tell it works
    Audits completed, age of voting equipment, and recovery exercises held.
    Reforms aimed at it
    • R-45 Sets the floor of paper records and audits that recurring grants would pay for.
  20. I032Late rule changes and slow rulings shake confidence in resultsC3 C4 C5 PlausibleWisconsin's ballot deadline changed in the final days before voting

    When voting rules change close to an election, voters and poll workers struggle to keep up. If disputes then take too long to settle, access suffers and fewer people accept the result.

    Where it happened

    Wisconsin's ballot deadline changed in the final days before voting Wisconsin, 2020.

    Five days before Wisconsin's April 7, 2020 election, a federal judge extended the absentee deadline and let ballots mailed after Election Day count. On April 6 the Supreme Court blocked that part, saying lower courts should not alter election rules on the eve of an election. Four dissenters warned that tens of thousands of voters might not get their requested ballots in time. Source: Supreme Court of the United States, 2020.

    A fix tried elsewhere

    Congress rewrote the electoral vote count rules in 2022 United States Congress, 2022 to 2025.

    The Electoral Count Reform Act, enacted in December 2022, limits the vice president's role in counting electoral votes to solely ministerial duties. An objection to a state's electoral votes now needs the signatures of one-fifth of both the Senate and the House, and only two grounds are allowed. Source: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School, 2022.

    Evidence
    Plausible. In Watson v. Republican National Committee (2026), the Supreme Court ruled that federal Election Day statutes do not bar counting mail ballots postmarked by Election Day, one example of rules litigated close to an election. No source listed for this record measures the effect of late changes on turnout or acceptance.
    Proposed response
    States, and Congress within its authority, would publish rules early and set up fast, neutral adjudication with clear certification deadlines and defined remedies. (States; Congress within authority)
    Tradeoff
    Emergencies still require limited exceptions, subject to court review.
    How to tell it works
    Rule changes made late in the cycle, contests unresolved at deadlines, and compliance with certification dates.
    Reforms aimed at it
    • R-45 Requires certification on a schedule, which narrows the window for late disputes.
  21. I048Court rulings limit what campaign-finance laws can doC1 C4 DocumentedSupreme Court struck down overall caps on giving

    Supreme Court rulings under the First Amendment have struck down many limits on political spending and contributions. Disclosure and public financing remain legal options, while broader limits would need a constitutional amendment.

    Where it happened

    Supreme Court struck down overall caps on giving U.S. Supreme Court, 2014.

    In 2014, the Supreme Court struck down federal caps on the total one person could give to candidates and political committees combined in a two-year cycle. Alabama resident Shaun McCutcheon and the Republican National Committee had challenged the 2012 cap of $117,000. The 5 to 4 ruling found the caps did not serve the only government interest the Court had accepted. Source: Federal Election Commission, 2014.

    A fix tried elsewhere

    New York State's match raised the share from small donors New York, 2024.

    New York State began matching small donations to legislative candidates in 2024, matching the first $50 of a constituent's gift 12 to 1. In the first cycle, 328 candidates took part. A Brennan Center study found that small gifts plus matching funds made up 45% of campaign money, up from 5% in earlier cycles. Source: Sludge, 2025.

    Evidence
    Documented. Citizens United v. FEC (2010) allowed unlimited independent spending by corporations and unions and upheld disclosure. McCutcheon v. FEC (2014) struck down aggregate contribution limits and held that only quid pro quo corruption or its appearance justifies limits. NRSC v. FEC (June 30, 2026) struck down limits on party spending coordinated with candidates.
    Proposed response
    Congress and the states would pursue disclosure and public financing now, and separately draft a constitutional amendment authorizing reasonable limits on political money with safeguards for speech. (Congress; states)
    Tradeoff
    Amendments are hard to pass, and vague language could give officials power to censor.
    How to tell it works
    A route to enactment, review for effects on rights, and durable compliance.
    Reforms aimed at it
    • R-07 Public financing is one of the tools current doctrine allows.
    • R-08 Disclosure survived Citizens United and is the other tool current doctrine allows.
  22. I072Unpredictable Supreme Court vacancies raise the stakes of each appointmentC1 C4 Well supportedOne president got no picks, another got three

    Justices serve for life, so the timing of deaths and retirements decides how many appointments each president gets. Recent confirmations have passed by near party-line votes.

    Where it happened

    One president got no picks, another got three United States (federal), 1977-2020.

    The Senate's list of Supreme Court nominations since 1789 shows none from President Jimmy Carter. Donald Trump's three nominees were confirmed in 2017, 2018 and 2020 by margins of two to nine votes. Barack Obama's 2016 nominee, Merrick Garland, received no Senate action and no vote. Source: U.S. Senate, 2026.

    A fix tried elsewhere

    Germany's top court judges serve one 12-year term Germany, Current rules.

    Germany's Federal Constitutional Court has 16 justices, and each one leaves after a single 12-year term or at age 68, with no second term allowed. Half are elected by the Bundestag and half by the Bundesrat, and every pick needs a two-thirds majority in the electing body. Source: Federal Constitutional Court of Germany (Bundesverfassungsgericht), 2026.

    Evidence
    Well supported. U.S. Senate records show recent Supreme Court confirmations passing by margins of 52 to 48, 50 to 48 and 53 to 47, close to party lines. The 2021 Presidential Commission on the Supreme Court reviewed proposals for term limits and for adding seats.
    Proposed response
    Congress and the states would compare regular 18-year Supreme Court terms, with transition rules, against amendment options, and publish standards for selecting nominees. (Congress; states)
    Tradeoff
    Term limits set by statute are constitutionally disputed, and adding seats to the Court can set off escalation.
    How to tell it works
    Predictable appointments, and the Court's legitimacy and independence.
    Reforms aimed at it
    • R-16 Regular 18-year terms give each presidential term two appointments, removing the role of chance vacancies.
  23. I073Supreme Court ethics complaints have no independent reviewC1 C4 DocumentedA justice took undisclosed luxury trips for two decades

    The Supreme Court adopted a code of conduct in 2023, and no outside body enforces it for the justices. When a court polices itself, complaints and conflicts can go unresolved.

    Where it happened

    A justice took undisclosed luxury trips for two decades U.S. Supreme Court, 2023-2025.

    In April 2023, ProPublica reported that Justice Clarence Thomas had accepted luxury trips from Dallas businessman Harlan Crow virtually every year for more than two decades without reporting them on his annual financial disclosures. Experts told ProPublica the law required disclosure of private jet flights. The article said the Supreme Court is left almost entirely to police itself, and Thomas publicly defended the trips. Source: ProPublica, 2023.

    A fix tried elsewhere

    Lower federal judges face a formal complaint process U.S. federal courts below the Supreme Court, 1980-2025.

    The federal courts' Table S-22 counts misconduct complaints against judges under 28 U.S.C. 351-364. In the year ending September 30, 2025, people filed 1,857 complaints. Chief circuit judges dismissed 1,700 in whole or in part, and three complaints were referred to special committees. Source: Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts, 2025.

    Evidence
    Documented. The Supreme Court adopted a Code of Conduct on November 13, 2023; it creates no independent process to decide complaints or enforce the code. Fix the Court, an advocacy group, reported in 2025 that the code remains unenforced, that the Judicial Conference dropped a referral concerning Justice Thomas, and that the Supreme Court Ethics, Recusal and Transparency Act had not been enacted.
    Proposed response
    The Supreme Court, or Congress, would publish reasons for recusals, review disclosures and create an independent complaint process consistent with judicial independence. (Supreme Court; Congress)
    Tradeoff
    A 2023 code already exists, and enforcement procedures have to avoid giving either party control over cases.
    How to tell it works
    Completeness of disclosures, and how complaints are resolved.
    Reforms aimed at it
    • R-16 Adds an enforceable ethics process for the justices.
  24. I149Hostility toward the other party leads voters to excuse their own sideC3 Well supportedFewer hardline Montana voters punished an attack on a reporter

    When partisans dislike or fear the other party, many will still vote for their own candidate after that candidate breaks democratic rules. That weakens the electoral cost of misconduct, though researchers dispute how much.

    Where it happened

    Fewer hardline Montana voters punished an attack on a reporter Montana, 2017.

    In 2017, Republican candidate Greg Gianforte body-slammed a reporter in his campaign office the night before Montana's congressional election, when more than half of voters had already cast absentee ballots. Yale researchers found that Election Day voters in politically moderate precincts punished him by voting across party lines, while significantly fewer did so in hardline Republican precincts. Source: Government Executive (republished from Yale News), 2020.

    A fix tried elsewhere

    Washington's climate assembly brought rival viewpoints to shared work Washington State, 2021.

    In early 2021, 80 Washington residents chosen by lottery spent seven weeks online writing climate recommendations for the Legislature. Evaluators from the Clinton School of Public Service reported a decrease in sensitivity to polarization and a willingness to work together among people with different viewpoints and political identities. Source: Clinton School of Public Service, University of Arkansas, 2021.

    Evidence
    Well supported. In Graham and Svolik's 2020 experiments, only about 3.5% of voters were willing to defect from their party's candidate over an undemocratic position in realistic matchups, although the average penalty in vote share was 11.7 points. Iyengar and colleagues (2019) review the causes and consequences of affective polarization, the dislike of the other party's supporters. Broockman, Kalla and Westwood (2023) found that affective polarization does not clearly reduce accountability, so the link is contested.
    Proposed response
    Civic groups, parties and local institutions would organize structured cross-party work on concrete shared problems and apply equal standards to political conduct. (Civic groups; parties; local institutions)
    Tradeoff
    Contact reduces hostility only under certain conditions, and surface civility cannot settle conflicts over rights.
    How to tell it works
    Attitudes toward the other party, joint work across parties, and consistent application of conduct standards.
    Reforms aimed at it
    • R-49 Cross-partisan membership and service is the structured contact this record proposes. Disclosure. Oath & Action's editor is an Army veteran.
  25. I150Scapegoating divides people who could work togetherC3 PlausibleBoston commuters grew less welcoming after brief contact

    Blaming racial or identity groups for hardship can pull attention away from the institutions that cause it. It also denies people equal standing and splits potential coalitions.

    Where it happened

    Boston commuters grew less welcoming after brief contact Boston area, Massachusetts, 2012.

    In July and August 2012, Harvard researcher Ryan Enos placed Spanish speakers working for his study on commuter rail platforms in largely Anglo-white Boston-area towns for 10 working days. Regular riders who saw them shifted toward wanting fewer immigrants from Mexico and opposing letting undocumented immigrants stay, though the effect may have weakened with repeated contact. Source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2014.

    A fix tried elsewhere

    Door-to-door conversations eased hostility toward immigrants for months Seven U.S. locations, 2020.

    In field experiments published in 2020, political scientists Joshua Kalla and David Broockman tested door-to-door conversations in which canvassers and voters swapped personal stories without judgment. Across three experiments, 230 canvassers talked with 6,869 voters in seven U.S. locations, and the first experiment reduced exclusionary attitudes toward unauthorized immigrants for at least four months. Source: American Political Science Review 114(2), 2020.

    Evidence
    Plausible. Sides, Tesler and Vavreck's Identity Crisis (2018) found from surveys that identity attitudes predicted vote shifts in 2016 more than economic distress did. In a field experiment, Enos (2014) found that brief exposure to members of an outgroup increased exclusionary attitudes.
    Proposed response
    Schools, civic groups and parties would protect equal participation and create local forums that connect material problems to evidence without blaming whole groups. (Schools; civic groups; parties)
    Tradeoff
    Dialogue requires safety and equal status for those taking part.
    How to tell it works
    Gaps in participation, and discriminatory incidents.
    Reforms aimed at it
    • R-49 Repeated shared work across groups is the kind of contact this record's response relies on. Disclosure. Oath & Action's editor is an Army veteran.
  26. I153Parties tolerate conduct that weakens democratic rulesC3 Well supportedEach party mostly shielded its own member from censure

    When voters rarely punish their own side, parties pay little price for nominating or protecting members who deny election results or intimidate opponents. Party rules and discipline are one place this can be checked.

    Where it happened

    Each party mostly shielded its own member from censure U.S. House of Representatives, 2021 and 2023.

    In November 2021, the House censured Republican Paul Gosar for posting a cartoon that depicted violence against Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez; 207 Republicans voted no and 2 voted yes. In December 2023, it censured Democrat Jamaal Bowman, who had pleaded guilty to falsely pulling a fire alarm; 191 Democrats voted no and 3 voted yes. Source: Office of the Clerk, U.S. House of Representatives, 2021.

    Evidence
    Well supported. Graham and Svolik (2020) found that only about 3.5% of voters would defect from their party's candidate over an undemocratic position in realistic matchups. Levitsky and Ziblatt's How Democracies Die (2018) argues from comparative history that party gatekeeping is a central safeguard. Bright Line Watch surveys of experts and the public track the erosion of democratic norms through 2026.
    Proposed response
    Political parties and civic organizations would adopt enforceable standards for nominations and conduct, with transparent disciplinary procedures. (Political parties; civic organizations)
    Tradeoff
    Gatekeeping needs internal democracy and due process.
    How to tell it works
    Compliance with party rules, and consistent sanctions.
