  27. I154Threats and violence raise the cost of public lifeC3 DocumentedThreats against Congress jumped to nearly 15,000 cases

    The U.S. Capitol Police opened 14,938 threat cases in 2025, the third straight annual rise, and 43% of state legislators surveyed reported threats. When serving in office or speaking up invites danger, fewer people take part.

    Where it happened

    Threats against Congress jumped to nearly 15,000 cases United States, 2025.

    In 2025, the U.S. Capitol Police's threat assessment unit investigated 14,938 concerning statements aimed at members of Congress, up from 9,474 in 2024. It was the third straight yearly increase and the highest count in the five years the agency reported. Source: U.S. Capitol Police, 2026.

    A fix tried elsewhere

    Capitol Police tripled local protection agreements in 2025 United States, 2025.

    In 2025, the U.S. Capitol Police tripled its formal agreements with local law enforcement agencies that help protect members of Congress in their home districts. It has also detailed its own attorneys to the Justice Department, where they have consulted with agents on 875 cases and worked on 1,705 subpoenas. Source: U.S. Capitol Police, 2026.

    Evidence
    Documented. The U.S. Capitol Police opened 14,938 threat-assessment cases in 2025, the third straight annual increase. In a 2024 Brennan Center survey, 43% of state legislators reported threats.
    Proposed response
    The Justice Department, the states and local law enforcement would fund lawful threat prevention, protect people who are targeted and prosecute violence under viewpoint-neutral standards. (DOJ; states; local law enforcement)
    Tradeoff
    Broad labels of extremism can chill lawful protest.
    How to tell it works
    Threat cases resolved, safety of victims, and public participation.
  28. I155Unsupported fraud claims weaken acceptance of defeatC3 DocumentedAppeals court refused to block Pennsylvania's 2020 certified result

    After the 2020 election, claims of fraud large enough to change the outcome failed in court, and a review by conservative lawyers found no supporting evidence in any of 64 cases. Such claims still threaten the peaceful transfer of power when officials act on them.

    Where it happened

    Appeals court refused to block Pennsylvania's 2020 certified result Pennsylvania, 2020.

    In November 2020, the Trump campaign asked a federal appeals court to stop Pennsylvania's certified presidential totals, a margin of 80,555 votes, from taking effect. The Third Circuit refused, noting the campaign "never alleges that any ballot was fraudulent," and Judge Stephanos Bibas wrote that "calling an election unfair does not make it so." Source: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit, 2020.

    A fix tried elsewhere

    Congress raised the bar for objecting to electoral votes United States, 2022.

    In December 2022, Congress amended the federal law for counting presidential electoral votes. An objection to a state's votes now needs the signatures of at least one-fifth of each chamber's members, and the vice president's role in the count is limited to "solely ministerial duties." Source: National Archives, Office of the Federal Register, n.d..

    Evidence
    Documented. The House Select Committee to Investigate the January 6th Attack on the United States Capitol issued its final report in 2022 on the effort to overturn the 2020 result. Lost, Not Stolen (2022), an independent review by conservative lawyers and former officials, found no evidence of outcome-changing fraud in any of 64 court cases.
    Proposed response
    Election offices, parties and courts would publish audit evidence people can understand, require officials to follow lawful certification and treat concession after a resolved contest as the norm. (Election offices; parties; courts)
    Tradeoff
    Legitimate challenges to results must remain available.
    How to tell it works
    Public understanding of audit evidence, and lawful transfers of power.
  29. I163At-will removal of regulators narrows agency independenceC1 C4 DocumentedTwo presidents removed FTC commissioners over policy

    In June 2026 the Supreme Court ruled that the President can remove FTC commissioners at will, and the same day left protection for Federal Reserve governors in place. Whether the change has altered enforcement priorities has not yet been measured.

    Where it happened

    Two presidents removed FTC commissioners over policy United States (Federal Trade Commission), 1933-2026.

    In 1933, President Franklin Roosevelt removed FTC Commissioner William Humphrey, writing that their minds did not "go along together" on the commission's policies. The Supreme Court held in 1935 that the law allowed removal only for cause. In June 2026, ruling on President Trump's 2025 firing of Commissioner Rebecca Slaughter, the Court overruled that decision 6 to 3, so FTC commissioners can now be removed at will. Source: Supreme Court of the United States, 2026.

    Evidence
    Documented for the legal change. In Trump v. Slaughter (June 29, 2026), the Supreme Court held the FTC's for-cause removal protection unconstitutional and overruled what remained of Humphrey's Executor, leaving the Federal Reserve and non-Article III courts unresolved. In Trump v. Cook the same day, the Court left removal protection in place for a Federal Reserve governor. The Congressional Research Service explains the ruling's scope and open questions.
    Proposed response
    Congress, agencies and the courts would protect statutory duties, require published reasons, keep records, protect professional case development and maintain congressional oversight, and would analyze the remaining tenure arrangements separately. (Congress; agencies; courts)
    Tradeoff
    Slaughter leaves Federal Reserve tenure and ordinary career-service protections undecided.
    How to tell it works
    Enforcement reversals made without explanation, vacancies, and compliance with review.
    Reforms aimed at it
    • R-48 Builds independence from records, public reasons for removal and agency structure after Slaughter.
  30. I165Small local governments lack money and expert staffC3 PlausibleThousands of rural communities lack staff to seek aid

    Towns with a small tax base often cannot afford the lawyers, engineers or procurement specialists their duties require. State grants and shared regional services are proposed ways to fill the gap.

    Where it happened

    Thousands of rural communities lack staff to seek aid United States (rural communities), 2026.

    Headwaters Economics, an independent research group, counts 7,886 U.S. communities with very limited capacity, judged by measures such as local government staff and expertise. Its 2026 index finds 46% of them face high flood risk, and it warns that many lack the staff and tax base to apply for federal programs. Source: Headwaters Economics, 2026.

    Evidence
    Plausible. Government Accountability Office simulations show persistent operating gaps in state and local budgets; they do not measure staff capacity directly.
    Proposed response
    States and local governments, with federal grants from Congress, would provide equalizing grants, shared professional services and regional technical help, with public accountability for results. (States; local governments; Congress for grants)
    Tradeoff
    Shared services can make government less responsive to each town, and recurring costs need steady funding.
    How to tell it works
    Services completed, fiscal stress, and staffing gaps.
  31. I166State takeovers move local decisions away from local votersC1 C4 PlausibleFlint's state-appointed managers switched the city's water

    States can override local governments or replace local boards, including county election boards. Power then shifts to officials whom local residents cannot vote out.

    Where it happened

    Flint's state-appointed managers switched the city's water Flint, Michigan, 2014 to 2016.

    In 2014, state-appointed emergency managers running Flint, Michigan, switched the city's water source to the Flint River. A task force appointed by Governor Rick Snyder found in 2016 that the managers made that decision in place of locally elected officials. It said the structure made it extremely difficult for Flint residents to check decisions. Source: Flint Water Advisory Task Force (State of Michigan), 2016.

    Evidence
    Plausible. Georgia's 2021 election law (SB 202) authorizes the State Election Board to take over county election administration; how often that power is used is the open empirical question. Grumbach's Laboratories Against Democracy (2022) documents declines in democratic performance at the state level and does not measure the effects of takeovers specifically.
    Proposed response
    State legislatures and state courts would require published criteria for any takeover, due process, a time limit and independent review, and would protect lawful local autonomy in state law. Residents would be able to invoke these protections. (State legislatures; state courts; residents)
    Tradeoff
    States hold broad constitutional authority over local governments, and its limits differ by state.
    How to tell it works
    Stated reasons for takeovers, outcomes of review, and voting access in affected places.
  32. I174A fixed-size House makes districts larger as the population growsC1 C2 C3 C4 PlausibleHouse districts have more than tripled in size since 1911

    The House has stayed at 435 seats for more than a century while the population grew, so each member now represents about 761,000 people. Larger districts go with less contact between residents and their representative.

    Where it happened

    House districts have more than tripled in size since 1911 United States, 1911 to 2020.

    Congress capped the House at 435 seats in the Apportionment Act of 1911, when the average member represented roughly 212,000 people. After the 2010 Census the average was about 710,000, and the Census Bureau put it at 761,169 after 2020. Source: U.S. House of Representatives, History, Art and Archives, 2026.

    Evidence
    Plausible. After the 2020 Census the average House district held 761,169 residents. Frederick (2010) found that larger districts go with less constituent contact and lower approval of the member; the evidence is observational and the effects modest.
    Proposed response
    Congress would evaluate expanding the House with a published apportionment rule, a plan for staff and facilities, and coordination with any change to how districts elect members. (Congress)
    Tradeoff
    More seats alone would leave disproportionality, gerrymandering and responsiveness unchanged.
    How to tell it works
    Residents per member, constituents' access to their member's office, and the cost of the transition.
    Reforms aimed at it
    • R-46 Adds seats so each member represents fewer people.
  33. X01In safe seats, a small primary electorate picks the winnerC1 C2 C3 C4 C5 Well supportedPrimaries with 7% of eligible voters settled most House seats

    In most House districts one party is sure to win in November, so its primary decides who takes office. Turnout in those primaries is a small fraction of eligible voters.

    Where it happened

    Primaries with 7% of eligible voters settled most House seats United States, 2024.

    Unite America, a group that advocates primary reform, calculated that 380 U.S. House seats, about 87%, were effectively decided in 2024 primaries. It found those primaries drew 18.1 million voters, about 7% of those eligible, and that 169 members ran unopposed in their primary for a safe seat. Source: Unite America, 2024.

    A fix tried elsewhere

    Alaska sends four finishers of any party to November Alaska, 2020 to 2026.

    Since 2022, Alaska has used one primary open to every voter in place of party primaries, and the top four finishers in each race advance to a ranked-choice general election. Voters approved the change in 2020. As of October 15, 2026, Alaskans decide on November 3, 2026 whether to repeal it. Source: Alaska Division of Elections, 2026.

    Evidence
    Well supported in direction. Unite America, which advocates primary reform, calculated that about 87% of U.S. House seats were effectively decided in 2024 primaries in which roughly 7% of eligible voters took part; the numbers depend on its threshold for a safe seat. Ballotpedia's 2024 competitiveness report separately counted 38 House races without major-party competition and found that 52% of incumbents faced no contested primary.
    Proposed response
    States, and voters by initiative where allowed, would adopt top-four or all-party primaries with ranked general elections, citizen redistricting commissions or multi-member districts. As of October 15, 2026, Massachusetts Question 3, on the November 3, 2026 ballot, would replace party primaries with a single primary in which the top two finishers advance.
    Tradeoff
    Parties lose control of nominations, and some voters lose a ballot line they value. Ranked counts take longer, and a primary that advances two candidates of one party leaves some voters without their party in November.
    How to tell it works
    Share of seats with a competitive general election, turnout in the round that decides the seat, and share of incumbents facing a credible challenger in November.
    Reforms aimed at it
    • R-01 Moves the deciding contest to a general election that all voters take part in. Disclosure. Oath & Action's editor works with the Yes on 3 campaign for Massachusetts Question 3 and promotes it through Veterans for All Voters, where he is Massachusetts state lead. He also co-leads Ranked Choice Melrose, a local campaign.
    • R-04 Commission-drawn maps reduce the number of seats made safe by design.
    • R-03 Multi-member proportional districts make most seats contestable even where geography sorts voters.
  34. X02States ban local voting methods and raise the bar for initiativesC1 C2 C3 C4 DocumentedOhio banned ranked ballots in every election, including cities

    Nineteen states now bar ranked-choice voting in some or all elections, including city elections. Some legislatures have also tried to make citizen initiatives harder to pass after voters used them.

    Where it happened

    Ohio banned ranked ballots in every election, including cities Ohio, 2026.

    Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine signed a bill on March 17, 2026, barring any election in the state from using ranked-choice voting. Cities that adopt it lose state local-government fund payments. Ohio became the 19th state with such a ban, weeks after Indiana enacted one in February. Source: Ballotpedia News, 2026.

    A fix tried elsewhere

    Ohio voters kept the majority rule for amendments Ohio, 2023.

    Ohio's legislature put a measure on an August 2023 special ballot that would have raised the vote needed to approve constitutional amendments from a simple majority to 60%. Voters rejected it, 57% to 43%, keeping the existing rule. Source: Ballotpedia, 2023.

    Evidence
    Documented. As of March 2026, 19 states prohibit ranked-choice voting by statute; Ohio's ban, signed March 17, 2026, followed Indiana's in February. Ballotpedia reports that 17 of the 19 bans were enacted where Republicans held the governorship and both legislative chambers. In August 2023, Ohio voters rejected, 57% to 43%, a legislature-referred amendment that would have raised the vote needed to approve constitutional amendments to 60%.
    Proposed response
    State legislatures, or voters by initiative, would protect cities' authority to choose their own election method and shield the initiative process from rule changes in the middle of a cycle.
    Tradeoff
    When cities choose their own methods, neighboring places can use different rules, which adds work for county election offices and for voters who move between them.
    How to tell it works
    States that ban local election methods, and initiative rules changed in the middle of a cycle.
  35. X03Off-cycle local elections draw fewer and different votersC1 C2 C3 C4 C5 Well supportedStand-alone city elections draw about half the voters

    Cities and school districts that vote in odd years or in spring draw a fraction of November turnout. The smaller electorate is older and more organized, and local decisions answer more to it.

    Where it happened

    Stand-alone city elections draw about half the voters California cities, 2022 study.

    Research reviewed by political scientists Zoltan Hajnal, Vladimir Kogan and G. Agustin Markarian finds that local elections held on the November ballot generally draw double the turnout of stand-alone local contests. In California cities, they found the off-cycle electorate was less representative of residents, especially by race and age. Source: Hajnal, Kogan and Markarian, American Political Science Review, 2022.

    A fix tried elsewhere

    California cities moved votes to November and widened the electorate California, 2022 study.

    California cities that moved their elections onto the statewide November ballot drew a broader set of voters. Using voter files, Hajnal, Kogan and Markarian found the on-cycle electorate was considerably more representative of residents, especially when local races coincided with a presidential election. Source: Hajnal, Kogan and Markarian, American Political Science Review, 2022.

    Evidence
    Well supported. Using California voter files, Hajnal, Kogan and Markarian (2022) found that moving city elections to the November ballot roughly doubles turnout and makes the electorate more representative of residents. Kogan, Lavertu and Peskowitz (2018) found that off-cycle school-district elections shifted the electorate and went with higher teacher pay than in on-cycle districts. Anzia's Timing and Turnout (2014) documents the turnout gap and the larger role of organized groups in off-cycle contests.
    Proposed response
    States by mandate, and cities through their charters, would move local elections onto the November ballot.
    Tradeoff
    Ballots get longer, and some voters skip local races listed below national ones.
    How to tell it works
    Local turnout, the mix of ages and of renters and owners among local voters, and housing approvals.
    Reforms aimed at it
    • R-06 Moves local elections to the November ballot, which is this record's response.
  36. X07State-level rules can weaken democratic accountabilityC1 C4 Well supportedUtah lawmakers replaced a voter-approved redistricting reform

    Some state legislatures have drawn maps that protect supermajorities, taken over local boards and overridden city rules on labor and housing. These state choices decide how much accountability voters have, whatever happens in Washington.

    Where it happened

    Utah lawmakers replaced a voter-approved redistricting reform Utah, 2018-2024.

    In November 2018, Utah voters passed Proposition 4, creating an independent redistricting commission and barring maps that unduly favor a party. In 2020 the legislature repealed and replaced it, and in 2021 lawmakers adopted their own congressional map, splitting Salt Lake County four ways. In July 2024 the Utah Supreme Court held that such voter reforms are protected from unfettered legislative repeal. Source: Utah Supreme Court (via Justia), 2024.

    A fix tried elsewhere

    New York's top court struck a partisan congressional map New York, 2014-2022.

    In 2014, New York voters amended their constitution to create an independent redistricting commission and ban partisan gerrymandering. When the Democratic-controlled legislature passed its own congressional map in 2022, the Court of Appeals struck it down on April 27, finding it was drawn with impermissible partisan purpose. The court ordered a trial court working with a special master to adopt new maps. Source: New York Court of Appeals (New York State Law Reporting Bureau), 2022.

    Evidence
    Well supported. Grumbach's Laboratories Against Democracy (2022) builds a state democracy index and documents declines in some states, including supermajority gerrymanders and preemption of city labor and housing rules. Georgia's 2021 SB 202 authorizes the state to take over county election administration. The Congressional Research Service has documented the mid-decade congressional redraws of 2025 and 2026.
    Proposed response
    State legislatures, state courts and voters by initiative would adopt enforceable districting criteria, limits on preemption and independent state election boards.
    Tradeoff
    A state that adopts neutral maps on its own can lose seats to states that do not, which invites retaliatory redraws.
    How to tell it works
    Partisan bias in state maps, preemption laws enacted, and takeovers of local boards.
    Reforms aimed at it
    • R-04 Independent commissions take map-drawing away from the supermajority the map would protect.
    • R-45 Sets a floor of lawful certification and protected officials that independent state election boards would carry out.
  37. X09Partisan identity weakens punishment of one's own sideC3 Well supportedOnly 3.5% would vote against their side to punish undemocratic conduct

    For many Americans, party has become a social identity tied to dislike of the other side. In experiments, voters penalized an undemocratic candidate from their own party, yet only about 3.5% were willing to switch their vote over it.

    Where it happened

    Only 3.5% would vote against their side to punish undemocratic conduct United States, 2020.

    In 2020, Yale political scientist Milan Svolik and coauthor Matthew Graham reported a nationally representative survey experiment in which Americans chose between hypothetical state legislative candidates. When candidates held their party's usual positions, only 3.5% of respondents would vote against their partisan interests to punish undemocratic conduct. Svolik said voters, regardless of party affiliation, are willing to forgive such behavior. Source: Government Executive (republished from Yale News), 2020.

    Evidence
    Well supported. In Graham and Svolik's 2020 experiments, a candidate's undemocratic position cost an average of 11.7 points in vote share, while only about 3.5% of respondents were willing to defect from their own party's candidate over it in realistic matchups. Abramowitz and Webster (2016) document the rise since the 1990s of negative partisanship, voting against the other party more than for one's own. Mason's Uncivil Agreement (2018) gives an identity-based account of polarization.
    Proposed response
    States, civic organizations and researchers would adopt electoral rules that reward building coalitions, support institutions that bring people of different parties together and use common-identity messages tested in the 2023 megastudy.
    Tradeoff
    Effects of cross-party contact and messaging fade quickly, within about two weeks in the megastudy.
    How to tell it works
    Cross-party membership, and measured animosity among members.
    Reforms aimed at it
    • R-49 Cross-partisan membership and civic service are the institutions this record proposes. Disclosure. Oath & Action's editor is an Army veteran.
    • R-02 Ranked ballots reward candidates who seek second choices from other camps. Disclosure. Oath & Action's editor works with the Yes on 3 campaign for Massachusetts Question 3 and promotes it through Veterans for All Voters, where he is Massachusetts state lead. He also co-leads Ranked Choice Melrose, a local campaign.
    • R-47 Fusion voting lets parties form coalitions behind one candidate. Disclosure. Oath & Action's editor works with the Yes on 3 campaign for Massachusetts Question 3 and promotes it through Veterans for All Voters, where he is Massachusetts state lead. He also co-leads Ranked Choice Melrose, a local campaign.
  38. X11Party organizations still steer who gets nominatedC1 C2 C3 C4 Well supportedAlaska's lieutenant governor quit a House race after the primary

    Party committees shape who runs and who survives a primary through endorsements, money and pressure on candidates to step aside. A June 2026 Supreme Court ruling lets parties coordinate unlimited spending with their candidates.

    Where it happened

    Alaska's lieutenant governor quit a House race after the primary Alaska, 2024.

    Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom, a Republican, finished third with about 20% in Alaska's 2024 top-four primary for the U.S. House, enough to advance, then withdrew. Many local Republican groups had endorsed Nick Begich, and a political consultant said two Republicans running against one Democrat would be a tough path. Source: Alaska Beacon, 2024.

    Evidence
    Well supported. On June 30, 2026, in NRSC v. FEC, the Supreme Court ruled that federal limits on spending parties coordinate with their candidates violate the First Amendment, overruling its earlier precedent. In Alaska's 2024 top-four primary, Lieutenant Governor Nancy Dahlstrom finished third with about 20% and withdrew, with Republican consultants citing the risk of two Republicans splitting the vote against one Democrat; it is a single case. The Party Decides (Cohen and colleagues, 2008) argues that party insiders effectively pick presidential nominees through endorsements before voters engage, a thesis contested since 2016 and limited to presidential races. Nineteen states ban ranked-choice voting by statute as of March 2026.
    Proposed response
    States and Congress would consider fusion voting and public funding directed to parties, require parties to publish their dues schedules, and treat party rules as part of the rules that govern elections.
    Tradeoff
    Fusion voting and party-centered funding can strengthen party leaders.
    How to tell it works
    Minor-party ballot lines that win votes, and how long coalitions last.
    Reforms aimed at it
    • R-47 Fusion voting and party-centered funding give organized coalitions a route that party committees do not control alone. Disclosure. Oath & Action's editor works with the Yes on 3 campaign for Massachusetts Question 3 and promotes it through Veterans for All Voters, where he is Massachusetts state lead. He also co-leads Ranked Choice Melrose, a local campaign.
  39. X15State supreme courts decide whether maps and voter-approved reforms take effectC1 C4 DocumentedVirginia's top court voided a voter-approved map amendment

    In 2026 the supreme courts of Missouri, Virginia and Utah decided whether new congressional maps and voter-approved changes would take effect. Spending on state supreme court elections reached a record $157 million in 2023 and 2024.

    Where it happened

    Virginia's top court voided a voter-approved map amendment Virginia, 2026.

    On April 21, 2026, Virginia voters narrowly approved a Democratic-backed amendment allowing congressional districts to be redrawn mid-decade. On May 8, the Supreme Court of Virginia struck it down 4 to 3, ruling that lawmakers first passed it after voting had begun in the 2025 House of Delegates elections. The current maps stay in place for 2026. Source: Virginia Mercury, 2026.

    A fix tried elsewhere

    Arizona voters kept retention elections for judges Arizona, 2024.

    Arizona voters decide whether to keep appointed supreme court justices in retention elections. In 2024, 78% of them rejected an amendment to end those votes. The Brennan Center reports that retention races have drawn less spending than contested elections, though an Oklahoma justice lost one in 2024 after $3.6 million in group spending. Source: Brennan Center for Justice, 2026.

    Evidence
    Documented. As of October 15, 2026, Missouri's Supreme Court upheld the 2025 mid-decade map 4 to 3 on March 24, 2026, then unanimously suspended it on September 3 until voters decide Proposition A on November 3, 2026. On September 10 the U.S. Supreme Court, with no public dissent, stayed a federal order that would have forced use of the new map, so Missouri votes in 2026 under its 2022 map. On May 8, 2026, the Supreme Court of Virginia ruled 4 to 3 that a redistricting amendment voters approved on April 21 was invalid because the legislature's first passage came after voting had begun in the 2025 House of Delegates elections. Utah's Supreme Court held in 2024 that the initiative power is constitutionally protected, and a trial judge imposed a court-selected map for 2026. The Brennan Center, an advocacy organization, counted $157.3 million spent on state supreme court elections in 2023 and 2024 across 79 seats in 35 states, a record, with interest groups outspending candidates for the first time.
    Proposed response
    State legislatures and voters would require disclosure of spending in judicial elections and consider merit selection of justices followed by retention elections. State courts would be treated as a check on maps.
    Tradeoff
    Merit selection moves the choice of justices further from voters, and disclosure rules raise privacy concerns for small donors.
    How to tell it works
    Share of judicial-election spending with an identified source.
    Reforms aimed at it
    • R-08 Disclosure of original funders applies to spending in state supreme court elections.

02.5

Reforms aimed here

10 reforms aim at a condition in Elections or at a connection that touches one. Each card says what it would change. Effects are rated family by family and never summed.

ReformR-01

All-party primaries with ranked general elections

Every voter, whatever their party, could vote in one first-round election, and two or more candidates would advance to a November ballot that all voters use.

Aims at L25 Decisive primaries reduce general-election pressure, L08 Safe seats make the primary decisive, C2 Seats settled in the primary

Expected effects, never added together

  • Democratic qualitymoderate positive
  • Government efficacysmall positive
  • Economic performanceno expected effect
  • Income and wealth equalityno expected effect
What it changes

In a safe seat the general election is predictable, so the party primary picks the winner (L08: Safe seats make the primary decisive). That weakens the threat incumbents face from the wider public (L25: Decisive primaries reduce general-election pressure). An all-party primary sends more than one candidate to November, which aims to lower C2: How often the primary decides the winner and raise C3: Risk of losing office. A top-two design advances two candidates; a top-four design advances four and can be paired with a ranked-choice general election. The reform sits on loop R10 (Safe seats shift accountability to small primary electorates), loop B4 (Electoral consequences can improve public performance) and loop R11 (Party loyalty weakens consequences for breaking norms).

Open the full reform, sheet 04

Disclosure. Oath & Action's editor works with the Yes on 3 campaign for Massachusetts Question 3 and promotes it through Veterans for All Voters, where he is Massachusetts state lead. He also co-leads Ranked Choice Melrose, a local campaign.

ReformR-02

Ranked-choice voting for single-winner races

Voters would rank candidates in order of preference.

Aims at C3 Risk of losing office, B4 Hostility to the other party

Expected effects, never added together

  • Democratic qualitysmall positive
  • Government efficacyno expected effect
  • Economic performanceno expected effect
  • Income and wealth equalityno expected effect
What it changes

Under plurality voting, two similar candidates can split their supporters and let a third candidate win; this is called the spoiler problem. Ranking removes that penalty, so more candidates can run, and it rewards candidates who seek second-choice support from other camps. The reform is linked to C3: Risk of losing office and to variable B4: Hostility toward the other political party. It sits on loop R10 (Safe seats shift accountability to small primary electorates) and loop B4 (Electoral consequences can improve public performance).

Disclosure. Oath & Action's editor works with the Yes on 3 campaign for Massachusetts Question 3 and promotes it through Veterans for All Voters, where he is Massachusetts state lead. He also co-leads Ranked Choice Melrose, a local campaign.

ReformR-03

Proportional elections in multi-seat House districts

Larger House districts would each elect several members, with seats shared in proportion to votes.

Aims at L42 Incumbent-drawn maps create safe seats, C1 Safe seats, D7 Entrenched majority control

Expected effects, never added together

  • Democratic qualitylarge positive
  • Government efficacydirection uncertain
  • Economic performanceno expected effect
  • Income and wealth equalitysmall positive
What it changes

Single-member districts let maps and the way voters cluster geographically produce safe seats (L42: Incumbent-drawn maps create safe seats). With several seats per district and a proportional count, most seats become contestable and the majority tracks the vote. The aim is to lower C1: Seats with little electoral competition and D7: Entrenched control of rule-setting institutions, even where geography sorts voters. The reform acts on loop R4a (Majorities draw maps that help them keep control), loop R10 (Safe seats shift accountability to small primary electorates) and loop R12 (Entrenched majorities shape courts that rule on election rules).

ReformR-04

Independent citizen commissions draw election maps

A commission independent of the legislative majority would draw district maps under explicit criteria, with public hearings.

Aims at L42 Incumbent-drawn maps create safe seats, L56 Durable majorities control maps and voting rules

Expected effects, never added together

  • Democratic qualitymoderate positive
  • Government efficacyno expected effect
  • Economic performanceno expected effect
  • Income and wealth equalityno expected effect
What it changes

A durable majority can use its hold on the legislature to draw maps and set access rules (L56: Durable majorities control maps and voting rules), and those maps produce safe seats (L42: Incumbent-drawn maps create safe seats). A commission cuts the step from D7: Entrenched control of rule-setting institutions to C4: Officeholders' control over election rules. It works through loop R4a (Majorities draw maps that help them keep control).

ReformR-05

Automatic voter registration

Eligible people would be registered to vote when they deal with a state agency, such as the motor vehicle office or a benefits office, unless they opt out.

Aims at L44 Restrictive access rules widen turnout gaps, B5 Equal turnout

Expected effects, never added together

  • Democratic qualitysmall positive
  • Government efficacysmall positive
  • Economic performanceno expected effect
  • Income and wealth equalityno expected effect
What it changes

Registration rules can lower turnout among the people they burden (L44: Restrictive access rules widen turnout gaps). Automatic registration removes one such cost. It aims to raise B5: Equality of voter turnout, where a smaller turnout gap between income groups counts as an increase. It operates on loop R4b (Voting rules shape who can hold rule-makers accountable).

ReformR-07

Public matching for small donations and vouchers

Candidates who join a voluntary program would receive public money that multiplies small donations, or voters would receive vouchers to give to the candidates they choose.

Aims at B1 Money spent on influence, C3 Risk of losing office

Expected effects, never added together

  • Democratic qualitysmall positive for entry; small negative for extremity
  • Government efficacyno expected effect
  • Economic performanceno expected effect
  • Income and wealth equalityno expected effect
What it changes

Public matching or vouchers change who funds campaigns (B1: Money spent to influence politics) and widen who can afford to run, which works on C3: Risk of losing office through more challengers. It touches loop B4 (Electoral consequences can improve public performance). Its target is candidate entry. Evidence does not show that it weakens loop R1 (Wealth and political influence reinforce each other).

ReformR-32

Public and philanthropic funding for local news

Public agencies and foundations would fund reporting on local government, with firewalls that keep funders out of editorial decisions.

Aims at B2 Local reporting, L26 Local reporting raises pressure on incumbents, LT03 Platforms drew ad revenue from local news

Expected effects, never added together

  • Democratic qualitymoderate positive if coverage restored
  • Government efficacysmall positive
  • Economic performanceno expected effect
  • Income and wealth equalityno expected effect
What it changes

Platforms took much of the advertising that once paid for local reporting (LT03: Platforms drew ad revenue from local news), and local coverage raises the risk officials face of losing office (L26: Local reporting raises pressure on incumbents). Funding with editorial firewalls aims to restore variable B2: Availability of local reporting, which rises with more reporters and falls as more counties lose their local source. It touches loop R16 (Local news loss and weak electoral pressure may reinforce each other) and loop B1a (Independent oversight can limit policy favoritism).

ReformR-45

Verifiable elections with paper records and audits

Every vote would leave a paper record, results would be audited, officials would face firm deadlines to certify, and election workers would be protected from threats.

Aims at B5 Equal turnout, E2 Earned trust, C5 Incumbents defeated

Expected effects, never added together

  • Democratic qualitymoderate positive
  • Government efficacysmall positive
  • Economic performanceno expected effect
  • Income and wealth equalityno expected effect
What it changes

Paper records, audits and certification on a schedule make results provable, so that C5: Incumbents defeated or pushed into retirement can happen and be accepted. Every reform that works through elections rests on this floor. The reform is linked to B5: Equality of voter turnout and to E2: Trust earned through performance, and to loop R4b (Voting rules shape who can hold rule-makers accountable) and loop B4 (Electoral consequences can improve public performance).

ReformR-46

Expand the House of Representatives

Congress would add seats to the House, so each member would represent fewer people, with a plan for apportionment and staffing.

Aims at C1 Safe seats, B5 Equal turnout

Expected effects, never added together

  • Democratic qualitysmall positive
  • Government efficacydirection uncertain
  • Economic performanceno expected effect
  • Income and wealth equalityno expected effect
What it changes

More seats mean smaller districts and more representatives per person, and pairing expansion with multi-member districts (R-03) multiplies the effect. The reform is linked to C1: Seats with little electoral competition and B5: Equality of voter turnout, and to loop R10 (Safe seats shift accountability to small primary electorates).

ReformR-47

Fusion voting and public funding for parties

More than one party could nominate the same candidate, so a voter could back a candidate on a smaller party's ballot line without splitting the vote.

Aims at C2 Seats settled in the primary, C3 Risk of losing office

Expected effects, never added together

  • Democratic qualitysmall positive
  • Government efficacyno expected effect
  • Economic performanceno expected effect
  • Income and wealth equalityno expected effect
What it changes

Fusion voting lets two parties nominate the same candidate, and party-centered funding helps organized coalitions form without spoiling races. The reform is linked to C2: How often the primary decides the winner and C3: Risk of losing office, and to loop R10 (Safe seats shift accountability to small primary electorates).

03.3

What holds it up

What the loop says

In a safe seat, the primary decides who wins, and few people vote in it. With little threat in November, officeholders answer to that smaller electorate and face less pressure from the wider public. Officials who cannot easily be removed can then write election rules that keep seats safe.

Loop R10 at a glance

Kind
Reinforcing, feeds itself
One turn
2 to 10 years
Now
Running up
Weakest step
L53, plausible
Reforms aimed at it
R-01, R-02, R-03

The weakest step

L53, Officials safe from defeat write rules for themselves, is graded plausible, which means some evidence. The loop holds only as firmly as this step.

Keep the qualification

Seat safety also comes from where voters live, and the claim that primary reform makes legislators more moderate is contested, so the loop concerns accountability more than ideology.

What the evidence shows

L08: Safe seats make the primary decisive and L42: Incumbent-drawn maps create safe seats are documented, and L25: Decisive primaries reduce general-election pressure is well supported. The weakest step is L53: Officials safe from defeat write rules for themselves, graded plausible: its evidence is the 2025 mid-decade redistricting in states with one-party control and legal analysis. Whether primaries make legislators more extreme is a separate, contested question, and the strongest tests found no effect.

How long one turn takes

2 to 10 years. L08 acts in under 2 years. L25 acts in under 2 years. L53 acts in 2 to 10 years. L42 acts in 2 to 10 years.

Where it stands now

Running up, measured by the share of House seats settled in primaries, 2012 to 2024. Improvement or decline can reinforce itself.

How to read the signs

Two of the four steps lower the next condition. An even number of lowering steps makes a loop reinforcing: it feeds itself. A plus sign means the two variables move the same way. It does not mean the change is good.

A real case

Alaska's top-four primary with ranked-choice general elections survived a 2024 repeal measure by 743 votes out of 321,203 after a December 2024 recount. As of October 15, 2026, a second repeal is on the November 3, 2026 ballot, combined with repeal of the state's rule requiring disclosure of the true source of political donations. One election cycle is too short to show the design's long-run effect on accountability.

04Reform R-01 · aimed at the safe-seat loop

All-party primaries with ranked general elections

ReformR-01 aims at L25, L08, C2 · band: rules

Every voter, whatever their party, could vote in one first-round election, and two or more candidates would advance to a November ballot that all voters use. In seats that one party usually wins, the choice now made in a low-turnout party primary would move to the full electorate. In Massachusetts, unenrolled voters already pick one party's ballot. Under Question 3, every voter would see all candidates on one primary ballot from 2028.

04.1

The problem it answers

R-01 answers loop R10, the safe-seat loop: In a safe seat, the primary decides who wins, and few people vote in it. Two issue records name the same problem. The problem evidence counts 2026 seats; the issue records quote their own examples, from 2024, so their counts differ.

Problem evidence, as of October 15, 2026

Plausible: some evidence

Cook Political Report rated 398 of 435 House seats safe for 2026, as reported by Unite America, an advocacy organization that funds primary-reform campaigns. Unite America's own count puts 383 seats (88%) as effectively decided in the 2026 primaries, which drew about 22.7 million voters, 9.4% of eligible voters. Both counts rest on ratings, which are forecasts, and on the group's definition of a safe seat.

Issue I026 · example from 2024

Closed primaries shut unaffiliated voters out of the deciding election

In a closed primary only voters enrolled in a party can help choose its nominee. Where the primary effectively decides the seat, unaffiliated voters have no say in the contest that settles it.

Millions of independents locked out of 2024 primaries. Unite America, a group that campaigns for open primaries, counted 15.7 million registered independents in 15 states who could not vote in their state's closed primaries in 2024. The group estimated that 87% of U.S. House races were effectively decided in primaries that year.

Why R-01 answers it: An all-party primary lets every voter take part in the contest that narrows the field.

Issue X01 · example from 2024

In safe seats, a small primary electorate picks the winner

In most House districts one party is sure to win in November, so its primary decides who takes office. Turnout in those primaries is a small fraction of eligible voters.

Primaries with 7% of eligible voters settled most House seats. Unite America, a group that advocates primary reform, calculated that 380 U.S. House seats, about 87%, were effectively decided in 2024 primaries. It found those primaries drew 18.1 million voters, about 7% of those eligible, and that 169 members ran unopposed in their primary for a safe seat.

Why R-01 answers it: Moves the deciding contest to a general election that all voters take part in.

In a safe seat the general election is predictable, so the party primary picks the winner (L08: Safe seats make the primary decisive). That weakens the threat incumbents face from the wider public (L25: Decisive primaries reduce general-election pressure).

04.3

What it changes

What it changes

In a safe seat the general election is predictable, so the party primary picks the winner (L08: Safe seats make the primary decisive). That weakens the threat incumbents face from the wider public (L25: Decisive primaries reduce general-election pressure). An all-party primary sends more than one candidate to November, which aims to lower C2: How often the primary decides the winner and raise C3: Risk of losing office. A top-two design advances two candidates; a top-four design advances four and can be paired with a ranked-choice general election. The reform sits on loop R10 (Safe seats shift accountability to small primary electorates), loop B4 (Electoral consequences can improve public performance) and loop R11 (Party loyalty weakens consequences for breaking norms).

How it would be put in place

Supporters first draft a measure and qualify it for the ballot, or a legislature passes a bill. A campaign follows. Before the first election under the new rules, election offices teach voters how the ballot works. After two election cycles, results can be judged by turnout in the round that decides each seat and by the number of contested general elections.

What it costs

Implementation is a small one-time cost for state and county election offices. In Massachusetts, Question 3 would take effect January 1, 2028, leaving time to prepare. Party leaders and incumbents who are secure in their primaries lose influence, first as a threat and in practice at the next open seat.

04.5

Routes and who can act

States set nomination rules for state and federal offices.

Who decides

States set nomination rules for state and federal offices. Where a state allows citizen initiatives, voters can change those rules at the ballot box, a route rated medium in feasibility for 2026 to 2030; as of October 15, 2026, Massachusetts Question 3 and Alaska's repeal measure are both on the November 3, 2026 ballot. Legislatures can act by statute, rated low because legislators elected under the current rules rarely change them. Home-rule cities can adopt the approach for municipal offices (medium) unless state law bans ranked ballots. Congress could act for federal races under the Elections Clause of the Constitution, which gets the lowest feasibility rating because most bills need 60 Senate votes while the filibuster stands (R-12).

The law

States control primary rules within limits the Supreme Court has set. In Jones (2000) the Court barred blanket primaries that force parties to accept nominees chosen by all voters. In Washington State Grange (2008) it upheld a top-two primary that does not name party nominees. A ranked general election also requires a state with no ban on ranked ballots.

04.6

Evidence for the problem and for the remedy

The atlas grades the problem and the remedy separately. A well-evidenced problem can have an unproven fix.

The problem

Plausible: some evidence

Cook Political Report rated 398 of 435 House seats safe for 2026, as reported by Unite America, an advocacy organization that funds primary-reform campaigns. Unite America's own count puts 383 seats (88%) as effectively decided in the 2026 primaries, which drew about 22.7 million voters, 9.4% of eligible voters. Both counts rest on ratings, which are forecasts, and on the group's definition of a safe seat.

The remedy

Contested: evidence disputed

More contested general elections and more candidates entering races are plausible results. Whether legislators become more moderate is contested: a 2014 study of state legislators by McGhee and colleagues found that more open primaries had little consistent effect on ideology, and experimental work finds that primary effects depend on conditions. Main limitation: Alaska's top-four system has a short record, so there is no long-run U.S. test of a top-four primary paired with a ranked general election.

04.7

Tradeoffs, risks and how to tell it works

Tradeoffs

Parties lose control over who carries their label, and some voters lose a party ballot line they value. Ranked tabulation takes longer to count. When two candidates from the same party advance, voters from the other party have no nominee of their own in November.

How it could fail

Party organizations in both major parties and incumbents secure in their primaries are expected to resist. Parties can coordinate so that only one of their candidates competes; in Alaska in 2024 one candidate withdrew after the top-four primary, with party consultants citing the risk of splitting the vote. Voters or legislatures can reverse the rule, and nineteen states ban ranked-choice voting in some or all elections. The reform can also fall short if turnout stays low in the deciding round, or if voters misread the ballot and trust in results drops.

How to tell it works

  • Share of seats with a competitive general election
  • Turnout in the round that decides each seat
  • Share of incumbents facing a credible general-election challenger
  • Voter understanding of the ballot, measured in exit surveys
  • Legislators' voting ideology, reported as exploratory because the best existing tests found no effect

Other options

Open partisan primaries let voters outside a party choose that party's ballot. Fusion voting (R-47) is another option, and proportional House districts (R-03) change the general election and leave the primary as it is. Two options are set aside as rejected. Blanket primaries are unconstitutional under Jones (2000). Turnout drives in closed-primary states raise participation and leave the rules on who may vote in a primary as they are.

Works alongside

R-04 Independent citizen commissions draw election maps, R-06 Hold local elections alongside November races, R-32 Public and philanthropic funding for local news.

04.8

Status and disclosure

Status, checked October 15, 2026

As of October 15, 2026, two measures on the November 3, 2026 ballot would change how primaries work. Alaska's Ballot Measure 2 (petition 24ESEG) would repeal the state's top-four primary and ranked-choice general election and return to party primaries. Massachusetts voters decide Question 3, which would replace party primaries for state and congressional offices with one primary listing every candidate, the top two advancing to November; if approved, it takes effect January 1, 2028. Nineteen states prohibit ranked-choice voting in some or all elections, by the National Conference of State Legislatures' count.

Sources in V7: W039, K1915, W040, K1700, W049, K1903.

05The loop catalog

Of 23 loops, 18 feed themselves and 5 push back.

A loop is a chain of causes that returns to where it started. 18 of the 23 feed themselves, so a change comes back stronger, and 5 push back. “Improvement or decline can reinforce itself.”

Every card draws its loop as boxes and arrows, read from the top; the return step closes it at the bottom. Two loops close only through an untested step, and 3 are sketches with no numbered chain. 22 of the 23 have at least one reform aimed at them.
